catalogTitle: הרמ"ח מצות הם רמ"ח איברין דמלכא. איברים בטלים לנפש לגמרי. כשעושים מצוה לשם שמים נעשה אז מרכבה לה'.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 23, the Rav explains that the 248 mitzvos are called the 248 limbs of the King because they are fully nullified to Hashem's will, so that one who does a mitzvah becomes a chariot for it, and one who learns Torah becomes truly united with Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling the Tanya's promise that serving Hashem is 'very near', and asks why it is so hard; the answer is the spirit of folly, which daas, holy understanding, removes. Turning to chapter 23, he cites the Tikkunei Zohar that the 248 mitzvos are the 248 limbs of the King, and stresses that this is a mashal, since Hashem has no body. He explains that the whole world is a mashal for spiritual matters, as Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim and Shir Hashirim show. Mitzvos are the inner will of Hashem, and all the upper worlds draw their life from the mitzvos done below. Just as a person's limbs obey his mind instantly, without deliberation, so the mitzvos and the body doing them are nullified to Hashem's will and become a merkavah, as the Avos were. Torah study is higher still: a full union with Hashem, even with the light that surrounds all worlds, hidden from us only by hester panim.

en: The Rav explains that serving Hashem is truly easy, and what makes it hard is the spirit of folly, which daas hakedushah removes.
Calling the mitzvos the 248 limbs of the King is a mashal, since Hashem has no body; the whole physical world was created as a mashal for spiritual matters.
The mitzvos are the innermost will of Hashem, and all the upper worlds, even the angels, receive their life through the mitzvos people do below.
Just as a person's limbs carry out his mind's will instantly without deliberating, the mitzvos and the limbs that do them are wholly nullified to Hashem's will.
When a person does a mitzvah, his limbs become a merkavah, a chariot, for Hashem's will, a taste of the level of the Avos.
Torah study is more than being a chariot: since every halachah is Hashem's will and wisdom itself, the one who learns is truly united with Hashem.
We do not feel this union because of hester panim, the concealment caused by the body and by sins.

bittul of the limbs to the soul
Torah study as union with Hashem

title.en: If it is so near, why is it hard?

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Tanya's promise to explain that serving Hashem is very near and easy, and asks why it is so hard; he answers with the spirit of folly and the need for daas. He then opens chapter 23 with the Tikkunei Zohar on the 248 limbs of the King, warning that Hashem has no body.

title.en: The whole world is a mashal

summary.en: The Rav explains that everything in the world is a mashal for a spiritual nimshal: Shir Hashirim, the Sfas Emes on reading it on Pesach, Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim, and even the sweetness of good foods as a mashal for the sweetness of Torah.

title.en: 248 limbs, 248 mitzvos and the tzelem Elokim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the 248 mitzvos are physical things, like tzitzis and tefillin, that hold spiritual lights beyond thought, and that man's 248 limbs correspond to them; this is the tzelem Elokim. The mitzvos are the inner will of Hashem.

title.en: The worlds live from our mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's will to do good draws life into all the worlds through the mitzvos done below, so that the Jew who keeps mitzvos is the soul of creation. Washing the hands in the morning purifies his part of the world from the night, when Hashem's name does not rest on darkness.

title.en: Limbs wholly nullified to the soul

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a child or student who pauses before obeying with a person's limbs, which carry out the mind's will instantly. So too the mitzvos, and even the body doing them, are wholly nullified to Hashem's will with no separation.

title.en: Becoming a merkavah like the Avos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the limbs doing a mitzvah become a merkavah for Hashem's will, as the Avos were at every moment. He illustrates the difference between contact and merkavah from the laws of tumah, and brings Yaakov Avinu, over whom Hashem stood as he slept.

title.en: Torah study: union, not only merkavah

summary.en: The Rav explains that thought and speech in Torah are the soul's inner garments, and that every halachah, kosher or pasul, is Hashem's will itself; since Hashem and His wisdom are one, one who learns Torah is not only a chariot but truly united with Hashem.

title.en: Hester panim and the light of sovev

summary.en: The Rav asks why one does not feel this union, and answers with hester panim, using a father watching his sleeping child and a dentist's anesthetic. He adds that the union of a Jew learning Torah is greater than that of the upper worlds, reaching even the light that surrounds all worlds, and that not feeling it is what keeps him from being consumed.

catalogTitle: מעלת התורה על המצות שהיא יחוד ממש בין ה' ובינינו. אם עושה עבירה ח"ו הוי יותר גרוע מהסט"א ממש.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why learning Torah unites a Jew with Hashem even more than mitzvos, and why a sin, which cuts him off from Hashem's will, makes him worse than the sitra achra itself, which never rebels against its Creator.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter 23: Torah study unites a Jew with Hashem more than other mitzvos, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not stop learning even for tefillah; the Arizal's statement that tefillah is central before Moshiach is like medicine for a sick man, not a ranking. Learning should bring great yirah, a yirah higher than the one that precedes learning, but most people today are numbed, like a patient under anesthesia, and do not feel it. Chapter 24 is the opposite: every sin, even against a rabbinic law, separates a person from Hashem's wisdom and is like idolatry, worse than the sitra achra, which obeys Hashem like Bilaam. The Rav shows how Hashem has the sitra achra given a small share: the goat to Azazel, tefillin hair, thirty-nine lashes, no matzah on Erev Pesach and the Magen Avraham's custom about kiddush. He warns that such customs need good sense, and ends with the laws of the bathroom.

en: When a Jew learns Torah he is united with Hashem's wisdom in a way beyond even the highest angels, more than through other mitzvos.
The Arizal's teaching that tefillah is central in the time before Moshiach does not make tefillah greater than Torah; it is what the present condition needs.
Knowing that learning unites one with Hashem should bring a higher kind of yirah, but people of our generation are numbed and do not feel it, though the bond is real.
Every sin, whether a Torah or a rabbinic prohibition, separates a person from Hashem's will and wisdom and is truly like idolatry.
The sitra achra itself never rebels against Hashem, since it knows its life comes from Him, so a sinner is worse than the sitra achra.
Hashem wants the sitra achra to keep a small measure of life until Moshiach comes, so the Torah has something given to it without offering to it.

tefillah in the time before Moshiach
kiddush and the hour of Maadim

title.en: Torah above mitzvos, and tefillah today

summary.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter 23: Torah study unites a Jew with Hashem beyond other mitzvos, which is why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not interrupt even for tefillah. He explains the Arizal's teaching that tefillah is central before Moshiach with a parable of a sick man who needs orange juice more than bread and meat.

title.en: The great yirah that comes from learning

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's point that knowing how learning unites one with Hashem should bring great yirah, distinguishes the lower yirah before learning from the higher yirah within it, and uses this to settle the Gemara's two statements about Torah and yirah. He then explains why most people today do not feel this yirah, comparing them to a patient under anesthesia.

title.en: A sin, even a rabbinic one, cuts off from Hashem

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter 24, the Rav explains that rabbinic laws are also Hashem's wisdom, entrusted to the sages of each generation, and that according to the Arizal they come from an even higher root. Therefore any sin separates a person from Hashem's will and wisdom and is like serving idols.

title.en: Worse than the sitra achra itself

summary.en: The Rav explains that in a sin the garments of the soul from kelipas nogah, and even the soul itself, become bound to the sitra achra. He then explains why the sinner is worse than the sitra achra: the Satan himself, with all his hosts, is subservient to Hashem and does His will.

title.en: Giving the sitra achra its small share

summary.en: The Rav brings Bilaam, who could not go against Hashem's word, and explains that the forces of evil depend on Hashem for their life. Hashem wants them to keep some life, and the Rav shows this in Purim, the goat sent to Azazel as the Ramban explains it, the hair at the tefillin, kaparos, the thirty-nine lashes as the Chasam Sofer explains them, and the Bnei Yissaschar's reason for not eating matzah on Erev Pesach.

title.en: Kiddush in the hour of Maadim, with good sense

summary.en: The Rav brings the Magen Avraham's custom not to make kiddush between six and seven on Friday night, the hour of Maadim, and the Aruch HaShulchan's sharp objection, and explains the Magen Avraham along the same line: the wine must not be taken wholly from the sitra achra. He adds that whoever keeps the custom must not make a hungry family wait, tells how the Chofetz Chaim made kiddush at once for a hungry guest, and concludes that everything must be done with sense.

title.en: The sitra achra's nourishment and the laws of the bathroom

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav reads that the kelipos are subservient to Hashem and draw their life from the 'back side' of His will. He explains why the laws of the bathroom are part of the Shulchan Aruch: the sitra achra draws its life from the waste, and so one may not think words of Torah there. He closes that nothing in Hashem's creation is in vain.

catalogTitle: כמו שהטוב הכי גדול היא קיום המצוה' כן להיפוך' הדבר הכי גרוע היא עבירה. איכות עוה"ז יותר רע מטוב' חוץ אצל צדיק.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 24, the Rav explains why a sin is worse than the kelipos and the lowest creatures, why this world is mostly evil and bitter except for the true servants of Hashem, and why a Jew who would die rather than serve idols still sins: a spirit of folly hides his hidden love.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the previous lesson: through a mitzvah a person is united with Hashem more than the highest worlds, while through a sin he is worse than the sitra achra, which still submits to Hashem; following the Ba'al Shem Tov, every sin carries a spark of idolatry. He then reads the Tanya's words that this world is the dregs of the kelipos, and shows from nature, from people and from each person's own reckoning that evil dominates here. Only rare tzaddikim truly taste the sweetness of Torah; he illustrates this with the Beis Aharon of Karlin, the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the cherries, and the tale of the king who sought a happy man's shirt. Returning to the text, he explains that the Tanya now answers how serving Hashem can be 'very near': a person sins only through a spirit of folly, which hides the love that would make him give his life rather than serve idols. Even wild animals obey Hashem, and they cannot harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim.

en: Through a mitzvah a person is bound to Hashem more than the highest worlds, while a sin cuts him off and makes him worse than the sitra achra, which still submits to Hashem.
In the upper worlds there is no evil, in the lower worlds good is the majority, but in this world evil dominates over good.
Only rare tzaddikim truly feel the sweetness of Torah and mitzvos; most people's lives hold more pain than pleasure.
Wealth, power and status do not bring contentment; only one who serves Hashem with truth and trusts in Him is truly content.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he sins only because a spirit of folly keeps him from seeing that every sin is also idolatry.
Even the wildest animals carry out Hashem's will, so the sinner is worse than them; and an animal cannot harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim.

the sweetness of Torah and mitzvos

title.en: A mitzvah unites, a sin is worse than the sitra achra

summary.en: The Rav reviews the previous lesson: through Torah and mitzvos a person is united with Hashem more than the highest worlds, while one who sins is the only creature that rebels against Hashem's will, worse than the sitra achra. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that thinking Hashem sees and lets the sin pass is a spark of kefirah.

title.en: This world, the dregs where evil prevails

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that this world is the dregs of the kelipos, explains the difference between ordinary waste and pure dregs, and shows that evil, absent above and a minority in the lower worlds, dominates here. He illustrates it from animals, from people, and from each person's reckoning of his own life.

title.en: Tzaddikim taste the sweetness of Torah

summary.en: The Rav says the exceptions are tzaddikim who feel the pleasure of Torah that Dovid HaMelech describes, while most people are not zocheh to it. He tells how the Beis Aharon of Karlin compared a poritz's extravagant summer sleigh ride to his own delight in Nishmas, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the free cherry: a taste is given as a sample, then one must pay with toil.

title.en: The great and wealthy are not content

summary.en: The Rav argues that this world is full of bitterness even for those who seem to have everything: world leaders, Napoleon who barely slept, the wealthy described in Likutei Moharan, and the statistics of suicide among the prominent. Only the Jew with bitachon who serves Hashem is content.

title.en: The king and the happy man's shirt

summary.en: The Rav tells a story he heard as a boy: a melancholy king was told to sleep one night in a contented man's shirt, but the only truly happy man his messengers found was a laughing beggar who owned no shirt at all. Wealth and power, he concludes, bring no contentment.

title.en: Serving with truth, and the Tanya's opening question

summary.en: The Rav says that one who serves Hashem with truth feels sweetness in a blatt Gemara, Tehillim, Shabbos and every mitzvah, but one should not expect the world itself to offer contentment. Returning to the text, he explains that the Tanya now begins answering its opening question from the title page: how can serving Hashem be 'very near'?

title.en: The sotah, the spirit of folly and the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that no one sins unless a spirit of folly enters him, learned from the sotah. Every Jew, even a sinner, has a hidden love that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he illustrates it with an angry father who snatches his child from a speeding car. So why does the sotah sin, when it is easier to resist adultery than to be killed?

title.en: A sin is worse than the lowest creatures

summary.en: The Rav explains that the spirit of folly covers the soul up to chochmah but not chochmah itself, so idolatry awakens mesirus nefesh; in truth even a light sin is idolatry and makes the sinner worse than impure creatures. He brings the Gemara that a gnat preceded the wicked, and explains that wild animals, though they have no choice, do Hashem's will, and that no animal may rule over a man.

title.en: Tzelem Elokim: the wolves and Daniel

summary.en: An animal kills a man only when he appears to it like a beast, having lost his tzelem Elokim. The Rav tells the Skulener Rebbe's family story of wolves that sniffed a wagon of holy children and left them unharmed, mentions Daniel in the lions' den, and concludes that the sinner rebels against Hashem more than the worst creatures, out of folly.

catalogTitle: דרשה לנשים: Shidduchim - of Sublime Origin; צניעות & חנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a shidduch is so heavenly that it stands above time and space, and that Chanukah, whose miracle came through Yehudis, is a time for women to strengthen tznius.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that the Torah records kfitzas haderech, a miraculous shortening of the road, only twice: when Eliezer went to find a kallah for Yitzchak and when Yaakov went to find his own. Everything in this world happens in time and place, but Shamayim is above both, and a zivug is a heavenly creation. This is why the bas kol that announces a match forty days before conception errs again and again, why the tenth of the ten utterances of creation begins with 'lo tov', and why, as the Tzemach Tzedek writes, the shadchan's small untruth is needed to bring the match down into this world. Turning to Chanukah, the Rav explains that women were the core of the miracle through Yehudis, which is why they refrain from work while the candles burn. Following the Chasam Sofer, their not lighting their own candles, rooted in tznius, is itself their publicizing of the miracle. He closes with the Shinever Rav on Eliezer's gift of clothing and a call to strengthen tznius.

en: Kfitzas haderech appears in the Torah only when Eliezer and Yaakov went to find a kallah, because a shidduch is heavenly and not bound by time and space.
The bas kol that announces a match errs repeatedly because a shidduch is too lofty even for a bas kol, which is only a daughter of prophecy.
The tenth utterance of creation, the creation of a partner for man, begins with 'lo tov', reflecting the wrong announcements that come before the right match.
Women were the core of the Chanukah miracle through Yehudis, and so their holiness on Chanukah is greater, shown by their refraining from work while the candles burn.
Women's not lighting their own Chanukah candles, which stems from tznius, is itself a publicizing of the miracle, since tznius was the miracle of Yehudis.

title.en: The sedra of the holy kallos

summary.en: The Rav opens in Yiddish with a mostly garbled reference to the Maggid of Mezritch and the aliyos of the sedra, then says this week's sedra is connected to kallos: it has four holy kallos, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah and Zilpah. He begins to mention two parshiyos with kfitzas haderech and is asked to speak in English.

title.en: Kfitzas haderech only for a kallah

summary.en: The Rav points out that the Torah records kfitzas haderech only twice, for Eliezer seeking a kallah for Yitzchak and for Yaakov seeking his own. He explains that this world has two vessels, time and place, which do not apply in Shamayim, and that every chasan and kallah is a new creation.

title.en: Only Hashem makes matches

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash of the queen who tried to pair a thousand servants and failed, and explains that a bas kol announces each match forty days before conception but errs many times first. He tells of the Sanzer Rav, who paid shadchanus even for failed suggestions, and asks why the bas kol makes mistakes at all.

title.en: Why the tenth utterance begins 'lo tov'

summary.en: The Rav answers that a shidduch is so heavenly that even a bas kol, a daughter of prophecy, cannot grasp it. He then shows that of the ten utterances of creation, only the tenth, the creation of a partner for man, opens negatively with 'lo tov', reflecting the bas kol's wrong announcements before 'matza isha matza tov'.

title.en: The shadchan's lie and the heavenly match

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tzemach Tzedek that a shidduch must be slightly blemished to come down into this world, which the shadchan's lie accomplishes, and this is why he is paid. For heavenly people like Eliezer's mission no lie is needed, and their journeys, being heavenly, were above time and space through kfitzas haderech. He tells the Neshei that in helping kallos they are partners in the tenth utterance of creation.

title.en: Chanukah, a yom tov of women

summary.en: The Rav explains that women are obligated in Chanukah lights though it is time-bound because they were part of the miracle, and that Tosafos brings the Rashbam that they were its core through Yehudis, who saved the Jews from a decree against their tznius. Measuring holiness by the prohibition of work, from Shabbos to Yom Tov to Chol Hamoed, he shows that women's refraining from work while the candles burn reflects their higher kedusha on Chanukah.

title.en: Why women do not light their own candles

summary.en: The Rav asks, with the Chasam Sofer, why women who were the core of the miracle do not light their own candles as mehadrin. The Chasam Sofer answers that the candles were originally lit outside and it was not tznius for women to join the crowd. The Rav asks why the Chashmona'im did not set it inside, and answers that the women's not lighting for the sake of tznius is itself the publicizing of Yehudis's miracle.

title.en: Tznius, Eliezer's gift and Moshiach's light

summary.en: The Rav says he cannot believe a report of immodest dress among the women, and brings the Shinever Rav that Eliezer's gift of clothing to Rivka was a sample of the tznius kept in Avraham's house. He calls Chanukah a time to strengthen tznius, cites the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah lights reveal the light of Moshiach, and closes with blessings to the Neshei.

catalogTitle: זה ספר לבינונים. מהו בינוני. השקפה נכונה למחשבות ותשוקות בלתי נכונות. אהבה ויראה לנשמות קטנות. לימוד תורה בהתמדה.

oneLiner.en: Opening the Tanya as a 'book of beinonim', the Rav explains that improper desires do not make a person less of an ehrlicher Yid, that the Tanya's short path to serving Hashem is meant for small people, and that even they can reach full, deep Torah learning through the hidden love every Jew inherits from the Avos.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the Tanya's three categories, tzaddikim, beinonim and reshaim, and explains that a person is created with a body and its desires in order to fight them: a desire for something improper means he is not a tzaddik, not that he is not an ehrlicher Yid, and the sin is only in letting the thought stay. He then reads the title page: a book for beinonim, gathered from seforim and from the Alter Rebbe's teachers, built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', with a long way through chapter 17 for those who can contemplate with chochmah, binah and da'as, and a short way from chapter 18 for smaller people. Reading chapter 18, he explains that the Torah speaks to the smallest Jew too, so even he can keep all the mitzvos, including talmud Torah, the hardest of them. A digression on the Gemara about interrupting learning for the Megillah teaches that bittul Torah is a matter of quality as well as quantity. He closes with the hidden love inherited from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, illustrated by a father who rescues his son from a fire.

en: A desire for something improper means a person is not a tzaddik, not that he is not an ehrlicher Yid; the sin is only in letting the thought stay in his head.
The Tanya, a book for beinonim built on 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', explains this closeness in a long way through chapter 17 and a short way beginning in chapter 18.
The long way is the Chabad path of contemplation with chochmah, binah and da'as that gives birth to love and fear of Hashem; the short way is for those too small for it.
The Torah is eternal and speaks to the smallest Jew as much as to Moshe Rabbeinu, so even he can keep all the mitzvos, including talmud Torah.
Bittul Torah is a matter of quality as well as quantity: learning less deeply than one could is a kind of bittul Torah.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem inherited from the Avos, which comes into the open when his bond with Hashem is threatened.

hidden love inherited from the Avos

title.en: Tzaddik, beinoni and improper desires

summary.en: The Rav sets out the three categories of tzaddikim, beinonim and reshaim and explains that a person is created with a body and its desires in order to fight them. Having an improper desire means one is not a tzaddik, not that one is not an ehrlicher Yid; the passuk 'velo sasuru' addresses such people, and the sin is only in letting the thought stay.

title.en: The title page: a long way and a short way

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's title page: a book for beinonim, gathered from seforim and from the Alter Rebbe's teachers, built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od'. He explains the long way of chapters 1-17, the Chabad path of contemplation with chochmah, binah and da'as, and the short way from chapter 18 for people who cannot use it.

title.en: Chapter 18: the word 'me'od' and small souls

summary.en: Opening chapter 18, the Rav asks how the Torah can call serving Hashem 'very near' when most people are not ovdei Hashem, and answers that the Tanya now addresses the person of limited understanding. He explains how chochmah and binah give birth to love and fear of Hashem, likened to a son and a daughter, and that this one cannot reach even the lower level of understanding it with his mind.

title.en: The Torah speaks to the smallest Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah is eternal and given to everyone from Moshe Rabbeinu to the smallest Jew before Moshiach, so even the smallest can keep all the mitzvos, even talmud Torah keneged kulam. Talmud Torah is the hardest mitzvah because every free moment, even a businessman's between customers, belongs to learning, and learning means understanding; reviewing a Gemara makes it clearer each time.

title.en: Bittul Torah in quality, not only quantity

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one interrupts talmud Torah for the reading of the Megillah and asks why that is bittul Torah when the Megillah is Torah too. With the example of a shopkeeper who opens his store but serves customers lazily, he answers that learning less deeply than one could is itself a kind of bittul Torah, and returns to the Tanya's point that talmud Torah demands one's whole mind and heart.

title.en: The hidden love inherited from the Avos

summary.en: Back in chapter 18, the Rav reads that even the small person can serve with his mouth and heart through the hidden love in the heart of all Israel, an inheritance from the Avos: love from Avraham, fear from Yitzchak, both from Yaakov. He illustrates it with a father angry at his son who still rushes into a fire to save him, and ends by announcing the schedule for next week.

catalogTitle: שורש ומהות של אהבה מסותרת. הם ירושה מהאבות' האבות הם המרכבה' יראת ה' ואהבת ה' נתאחדו בגופם ונמשכו לבניהם.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter 18: every Jew carries a hidden love and fear of Hashem as an inheritance from the Avos, an instinct as natural as the inherited knowledge of animals, because the Avos were a chariot for the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews how the first seventeen chapters of Tanya explain the verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' through contemplation, and opens chapter 18, which shows that even a simple person who cannot arouse love and fear can serve Hashem through the hidden love inherited from the Avos. To explain inheritance, he shows from nature that physical traits and instinctive knowledge pass to offspring (the bee's honeycomb, the beaver's dam, the spider's web) while acquired wealth and learning do not. A Jew's emunah is such an instinct, inherited from Avraham, whose creation completed the world. Sins can cover it, and people deny their belief to excuse their desires, as Esav and Chiel did. The Jewish body too is suited for kedushah; a convert receives a new body through tevilah, whose essence is self-nullification. Finally, love and fear are inherited because the Avos were a merkavah, wholly nullified to Hashem.

en: Tanya chapter 18 teaches that even a simple person who cannot arouse love and fear through contemplation can serve Hashem with them, through the hidden love inherited from the Avos.
In nature, physical traits and certain instinctive knowledge pass by inheritance, while things acquired from outside, like wealth or learning, do not.
A Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, part of his very makeup, so that even a Jew who says he does not believe really does.
Emunah can be weakened by sin, like a spoiled appetite, and people deny their belief to excuse their desires, but it can be restored.
The Avos were a merkavah, a chariot wholly nullified to Hashem, constantly in love and fear, and therefore drew their nefesh, ruach and neshamah to all their descendants.

title.en: Review and the opening of chapter 18

summary.en: The Rav reviews how the first seventeen chapters explain 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' through contemplating Hashem's greatness, which gives birth to love and fear. He then reads the opening of chapter 18: for a simple person, or a dulled generation, who cannot reach love and fear even intellectually, there is the hidden love in every Jew's heart, inherited from the Avos.

title.en: What passes by inheritance in nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Hashem's nature traits pass by inheritance: hair color follows a known formula, a fine tree's seed gives fine fruit. Acquired things like money or knowing a masechta do not pass, but certain instinctive knowledge does: the bee's honeycomb, the beaver's dam and the spider's web are built by young that never saw their parents do it.

title.en: Emunah as an inheritance from Avraham

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew's emunah passes by inheritance from Avraham Avinu, so every Jew believes instinctively, while a non-Jew must come to belief through contemplation and resists because it does not suit him, as the nations refused the Torah. Apart from rare exceptions of a misplaced soul, even a Jew who says he does not believe carries the belief in his blood.

title.en: Weakened emunah and self-deception

summary.en: The Rav compares emunah to appetite: a spoiled stomach dulls it, and sins can weaken emunah, but a tzaddik, a mussar sefer or teshuvah restores it. He then shows how people deceive themselves and blame anything but themselves, with the hammer, yeshiva bochurim, Esav taking Machalas, a man of desire who claims heresy, and Chiel of Beis HaEli who rebuilt Yericho and explained away his children's deaths.

title.en: The creation of Avraham and the letter hei

summary.en: The Rav explains that after 'Vayechulu' creation was not yet complete: Chazal read 'behibaram' as 'b'Avraham', a new creature who believed in Hashem instinctively. The hei, which the Zohar calls the letter of birth, was added to his name so his emunah would pass to his children, as the morning verses say 'v'samta shmo Avraham' and 'his heart was faithful'. That emunah can be covered, like a spoiled stomach, but it remains.

title.en: The Jewish body and the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's body comes from kelipas nogah and is suited for kedushah, its 248 limbs matching the 248 positive mitzvos. The love is revealed or hidden, but a great test awakens it even in a rasha. He then reads the Tanya text: from Avraham the trait of love, from Yitzchak fear, from Yaakov mercy, and the hidden love in the heart of all Israel is our inheritance.

title.en: The convert's new body and the mikvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a convert has a Jewish soul but a body born of a non-Jew, and through milah and tevilah receives a new body. Bringing the Baal Shem Tov's kavanos of mikvah from the Baal HaTanya's siddur and the Arizal, he explains that tevilah is a rebirth through self-nullification, like a curled-up fetus. He rejects a shortcut of many quick tevilos with a finger, and says one should do teshuvah before Shabbos as if converting anew.

title.en: The Avos are the merkavah

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's question: how can love born from contemplation be inherited, and how can fear, its opposite, be included in it? The answer is that the Avos were the merkavah: never separated from Hashem for a moment, always in love and fear, wholly nullified like a chariot to its rider, and more than the mashal shows. Therefore they drew their nefesh, ruach and neshamah, with emunah that includes love and fear, to all their descendants forever.

catalogTitle: Current Events: The Recession - Give צדקה with שמחה. The קדושים of the Mumbai Massacre

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that a Jew who sees every event, even a recession or the killing of the Mumbai kedoshim, as coming from Hashem for his good will serve Him with simcha, and above all give tzedakah gladly.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Mizmor Lesodah: one who appreciates the hidden miracles Hashem does for him every moment thanks Him in hard times as in good ones, and serves Him with simcha. Citing the Reishis Chochmah that a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more, he turns to the poor who interrupt davening: the collector is a messenger bringing a gift that may save the giver. Now that a recession has been announced, the needy are needier than ever and tzedakah matters more. He then speaks of the Mumbai kedoshim, the shluchim who hosted guests in India. Answering why it happened with Hashem's reply to Moshe Rabbeinu about Rabbi Akiva, he brings the Zohar on the place of those killed as Jews, and says they remain on their shlichus before Moshiach. He closes with the hidden miracles of the body, a warning about the dangerous times, and stories of tzaddikim whose joy in mitzvos surpassed every worldly pleasure.

en: One who realizes that every breath and heartbeat is a hidden miracle from Hashem thanks Him for the hard as for the good, and serves Him with simcha.
Following the Reishis Chochmah, the Rav says a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more in Heaven, so a dollar given gladly outweighs a hundred given grudgingly.
The poor man who interrupts one's davening is a messenger from Hashem bringing a gift, and the Rav says one should not see him as a disturbance.
In the recession it is harder but more important to give tzedakah, because the needy are needier than ever.
The Mumbai killing must be accepted with the answer Moshe Rabbeinu received about Rabbi Akiva: it is part of Hashem's plan, which will be understood in its time.
According to the Zohar, a Jew killed because he is a Jew goes straight to the heichal of Moshiach, the highest chamber in Gan Eden.
The Rav says the times are dangerous and one must prepare by doing mitzvos, welcoming every small mitzvah as a gift.

title.en: Mizmor Lesodah: thanks for hidden miracles

summary.en: Continuing Mizmor Lesodah, the Rav explains that one who appreciates the hidden miracles Hashem does every moment calls on His name in distress as in salvation, and serves Him with simcha. He brings the Reishis Chochmah that a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more.

title.en: The poor man at davening and the recession

summary.en: The Rav describes collectors who interrupt davening and those who give grudgingly, and teaches that each poor man is Hashem's messenger bringing a gift that may save the giver. With a recession announced, he says tzedakah is harder but more important, and the collector should not be seen as a disturbance.

title.en: The Mumbai killing and Hashem's hidden plan

summary.en: The Rav calls the Arab terrorists a 'pere adam', tells of the Chofetz Chaim's words to a man moving to Eretz Yisroel after the Tarpat pogroms, and turns to the couple killed in India after hosting many guests. To the question why, he brings Hashem's answer to Moshe Rabbeinu about Rabbi Akiva's death: be silent, this is the plan.

title.en: The place of those killed as Jews

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a Jew killed for being a Jew goes straight to the heichal of Moshiach and his name is inscribed on Hashem's garment of vengeance. He adds that great tzaddikim longed to die al kiddush Hashem, bringing the Beis Yosef's Maggid Meisharim, where the angel told him he lost that chance through extra wine.

title.en: Shluchim still on their shlichus; the two worms

summary.en: The Rav says the shluchim of the Lubavitcher Rebbe are still on their shlichus, and tells of a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov who met Avraham Avinu on the road asking for the redemption; the shluchim should now tell Moshiach the truth about Jews in India. He then tells the parable of the worm in the radish who cannot imagine a strawberry.

title.en: The tzaddik's level and giving with simcha

summary.en: The Rav explains that a great tzaddik feels the bad is as good as the good, while the Gemara's separate berachos speak to ordinary people. He stresses that he is only repeating what the sefarim demand: simcha and bitachon, and giving the poor man's dollar with simcha, which by the Reishis Chochmah becomes a thousand dollars.

title.en: Miracles of the body and a dangerous world

summary.en: The Rav describes the constant hidden miracles of the body, adding that one who never needed rescue has a bigger miracle than those who bring a korban todah. He warns that the world is a barrel of dynamite with a lit wick, brings the Navi's call to seek righteousness, and urges welcoming every small mitzvah, like the dollar for tzedakah, as a gift.

title.en: Stories: the joy of a mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav tells three stories: Reb Avraham of Ciechanow, who felt more joy putting on tefillin than his friend did winning a lottery; the Kedushas Levi asking whether a luxurious paritz lights Chanukah candles; and a Rebbe who said a paritz sledding on sacks of sugar has no pleasure like his own in saying Nishmas on Shabbos morning.

catalogTitle: יש יראה ואהבה ביחד רק בה'. אבות נתאחדו בה' יותר ממרכבה גשמית. לפי שהאבות היו בעצם אלקות לכן בניהם גם הם כן. אין מקיף אם אינו מחובר לפנימיות. ביאור קצרה בד' עולמות וי' ספירות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 18, the Rav explains why love and fear of Hashem can live together only with Hashem, how the avos became so united with Him that this bond passed to their children, and gives a short explanation of the four worlds and the ten sefiros.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that every Jew inherits a hidden love from the avos: love is the trait of Avraham and of Beis Hillel, fear that of Yitzchak and of Beis Shammai. Positive mitzvos come from love and prohibitions from fear, which is why a positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition, as he shows from the Ramban on zachor and shamor and from the Gemara on tzitzis and shaatnez. He then asks how fear, the opposite of love, can be part of the same inheritance, and answers that only with Hashem can union and awe coexist. The avos were Hashem's merkavah, yet more united than a chariot with its rider; their bond became their very essence and so passed to their children, together with nefesh, ruach and neshamah, even where these remain hidden as a makif. Finally he explains the ten sefiros and four worlds through the mashal of vapor, steam, water and ice, and the human powers of the soul, ending with daas.

en: Love is the trait of Avraham and Beis Hillel, fear the trait of Yitzchak and Beis Shammai; positive mitzvos stem from love and prohibitions from fear.
A positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition because love is greater than fear.
Love and fear can coexist without contradiction only toward Hashem: union with Him and nullification before Him go together.
The avos were completely nullified to Hashem, more united with Him than a chariot with its rider, and so they drew down nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children.
Only a trait that is part of a person's essence is inherited; the avos' bond with Hashem became their essence, so their children inherit a hidden love.

The ten sefiros come down through the four worlds of Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah by ever greater tzimtzum, like vapor that becomes steam, water and ice, and in man they become the ten powers of the soul.
Daas is the bridge between the intellect and the midos: it knows when to use each trait.

daas as the bridge between mind and midos

title.en: Love and fear as the traits of the avos

summary.en: The Rav reviews that every Jew has a hidden love inherited from the avos and asks what its root is. He links love to Avraham and Beis Hillel and fear to Yitzchak and Beis Shammai, and says positive mitzvos come from love and prohibitions from fear.

title.en: Why a positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban on zachor and shamor: a positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition because love is greater than fear. He contrasts another view that action is greater than refraining, and shows the Gemara's source from tzitzis of wool on a linen garment.

title.en: Love and fear together, and the avos as merkavah

summary.en: The Rav asks how fear, the opposite of love, can be part of the inherited love, and answers that only toward Hashem can union and awe coexist. He explains that the avos, as Hashem's merkavah, had no will of their own and drew nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children, like a horse that does only what its rider wants.

title.en: The limit of a mashal: more than a chariot

summary.en: The Rav shows from Dovid HaMelech comparing himself to a desert bird that a mashal holds only in one detail. A chariot can be separated from its rider, but the avos were united completely with Hashem and became a level of Elokus, which is why they passed nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children.

title.en: What is inherited: essence, and the hidden makif

summary.en: The Rav explains that only essential traits are inherited, and the avos' bond with Hashem became their essence. He describes when one receives nefesh, ruach and neshamah, and explains through a mashal of hair color that ruach and neshamah held hidden as a makif, connected to a person's inner self, can come out in his children.

title.en: The ten sefiros and tzimtzum

summary.en: The Rav begins explaining the ten sefiros: the first powers Hashem drew forth at creation, named for the brilliant sapphire stone. Man, made in Hashem's image, has their reflection as his midos, and the great light was contracted and clothed again and again so the lower worlds could bear it.

title.en: The mashal of vapor, steam, water and ice

summary.en: To explain hishtalshelus and tzimtzum the Rav gives the mashal of a boiling kettle: invisible vapor near the spout, then steam that has no substance, then water that takes no form, then ice that can be shaped and touched. It is all the same thing, only ever more physical.

title.en: The four worlds and the names of the sefiros

summary.en: The Rav applies the mashal: the light was contracted step by step into Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, each world able to create what the one above could not, until physicality is possible. The four worlds match the four letters of Hashem's Name, and he lists the ten sefiros.

title.en: Chochmah, binah, daas and the midos in man

summary.en: The Rav explains the powers of the soul: chochmah as the flash of an idea, binah as building it out, the midos from chesed to malchus, and daas as the bridge that knows when to use each trait. A child can be clever yet not a ba'al daas until he becomes bar mitzvah.

catalogTitle: אצילות' ד' עולמות והשתלשלות איך עובדים ביחד. יש כמה מדריגות בנשמות אבל הנקודה של אברהם אבינו בכולם. נשמה ממדריגה נמוכה ביותר יכול להוליד נשמות גבוהות כי בתוכו מדריגת כתר. זה ענין מחול.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how G-d's light descends through the four worlds and the levels of souls, and shows that beneath all the outer differences every Jew holds the same inner point from the Avos, which is revealed in the round dance and on Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the ten sefiros, which match a person's ten powers of the soul and the ten utterances of Creation, and explains hishtalshelus, the descent of G-d's light, with a mashal of vapor turning into water and ice and of dark film used to watch an eclipse. The four worlds, Atzilus, Beriyah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, act as curtains, and each holds ten sefiros. Souls also come from these worlds, in some forty general levels, yet every Jew carries an inner point inherited from the Avos. With a mashal of coated aspirin and of inherited hair color he shows that the differences are only in the outer garments. Reading Tanya chapter 18, he explains that even the lowest Jew has chochmah within, because holiness is unity. From here he explains the round dance, machol, where all stand equally near Hashem, the mechilah of Yom Kippur, and the verse calling the Jews 'bnei kushiyim'.

en: G-d's light comes down through the four worlds, each acting as a curtain that dims it, so that the lower worlds and man can receive it.
Souls come from the four worlds in about forty general levels, from Chochmah of Atzilus down to Malchus of Asiyah, with countless finer levels within them.
Every Jew has an inner point inherited from the Avos, and in that point all Jews are equal; the differences between them are only in the outer garments.
Following Tanya chapter 18, even the lowest Jew, whose soul is nefesh of nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah, holds within him chochmah in which the light of Ein Sof shines.
Holiness is unity and impurity is division, so a Jew can connect to the Avos only when he is united with other Jews.
The round dance, machol, reveals the inner equality of all Jews, and the same revelation brings the mechilah of Yom Kippur.

candidateTopics: inner point inherited from the Avos

title.en: Ten sefiros and the descent of light

summary.en: The Rav reviews the ten sefiros and the ten powers of the soul, links them to the ten utterances, ten plagues and ten commandments, and explains hishtalshelus with water turning from vapor to ice. He adds that creation cannot receive a light that is too strong, like the sun during an eclipse, which is watched through layers of dark film.

title.en: The four worlds as curtains

summary.en: The Rav explains the four worlds, matching the four letters of Hashem's name, and derives the name Atzilus from 'etzel', near, like the nobles near the king. Each world is a curtain that lets through only a little light, each holds ten sefiros, and together they form Hashem's reshus hayachid, ten high and four wide.

title.en: Levels of souls and the inner point

summary.en: The Rav explains that souls too come from the four worlds, from souls of Atzilus like Moshe Rabbeinu and the Avos down to the lowest level, nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah, in about forty general levels. Yet every Jew, even an am ha'aretz, has hidden within him the point he inherited from the Avos, and in it all are equal.

title.en: The mashal of the coated aspirin

summary.en: The Rav gives a long mashal of an aspirin with a sweet coating over an enteric coating, so that it passes the mouth and the stomach unharmed and acts only in the intestines; under both coatings it is still aspirin. So too every Jew's inner point from the Avos is the same under coarse or refined garments, and he adds a mashal of hair color hidden in one generation and revealed in the next.

title.en: Tanya ch. 18: chochmah in the lowest Jew

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 18: the Avos are the merkavah and drew down nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children from the four worlds, and even the lowest Jew has nefesh of nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah. Because in holiness all is unity, unlike the division of the sitra achra, this lowest level contains chochmah and the light of Ein Sof, as in 'Hashem bechochmah yasad aretz'.

title.en: The round dance of the tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara at the end of Taanis that Hashem will make a dance, machol, for the tzaddikim, and explains with the Chasam Sofer that in a round dance, as at a round table, everyone is equal and equally near Hashem in the center. Therefore a chassidic dance is a high avodah, one must not talk during it, and the dancers must hold hands like an unbroken electric circuit, as the Baal Shem Tov did.

title.en: Machol, mechilah and bnei kushiyim

summary.en: The Rav connects machol with mechilah: on Yom Kippur the inner point of every Jew is revealed, and that is why he is forgiven. He then explains the verse calling the Jews 'bnei kushiyim': as with skin color, the difference is only on the surface, and beneath it every Jewish soul is a part of G-d above. He closes by noting that the next chapter of Tanya builds on this introduction.

catalogTitle: טעם שאפי' פושעים מולידים נשמות גדולות. חכמה למעלה מהשגה. פילפולי התורה מבינים אבל גזירות אינם מבינים. חכמה מקור הבינה. יארצייט המגיד ממזריטש זצוקללה”ה שהוא מקור החסידות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 18, the Rav explains why great souls are often born to simple Jews, why the darkest times bring the light of Moshiach as Chanukah does, and why chochmah, the source of binah, is beyond understanding.

abstract.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 18: even the lowest Jew has in his inwardness the highest level, and great souls are born even to simple people, as the Sefer HaGilgulim says. He explains that the hidden inheritance of the Avos surfaces in later generations, and that Hashem hides great souls among simple or sinful parents to outwit the Satan, as seen in the lineage of David HaMelech and a Midrash about Esav and David. He connects this to Chanukah, which falls in Teves, the hardest month and the longest night, and reveals a spark of the light of Moshiach, as will happen in the darkness of ikvesa dimeshicha. Today's trials are great, but like a stone dropped from high that sinks deep, today's souls fell from high places. Returning to Tanya, he explains through a river's hidden spring and an inventor who cannot explain gravity that chochmah is the source of binah and cannot be grasped. He closes with the yahrzeit of the Maggid of Mezritch.

en: Even the lowest Jew carries in his inwardness the highest levels, the inheritance of Avraham Avinu, which can surface in his children or grandchildren.
Hashem brings great souls through simple or sinful parents to outwit the Satan, who would never think to look there.
Chanukah comes at the lowest point of the year, in Teves and its longest night, and its lights reveal a spark of the light of Moshiach, just as Moshiach will be revealed in the lowest generation.
The souls of the generation before Moshiach fell from very high places and therefore sank deep, so they can raise sparks that earlier generations could not reach.
Chochmah is the source of binah and is beyond grasp: one can understand and explain what is built on the first point, but not the point itself.

chochmah as the source of binah

title.en: Why simple people have great children

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 18, that even the lowest soul holds within it the highest level and that great souls are born to simple people. He explains that the hidden inheritance of the Avos surfaces in later generations, like a talent for niggun that skips a generation.

title.en: Outwitting the Satan: the line of David

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem uses this to trick the Satan, as seen in the lineage of David HaMelech. He brings a Midrash that the Satan hoped for a share through Esav and later through David, who was also 'admoni', and compares it to an owner who hides his diamonds where a thief will not look.

title.en: Chanukah in the darkest night

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Teves belongs to Esav and is the hardest month, and that its long night is the time the sitra achra rules. Chanukah comes precisely then and its lights reveal a spark of the light of Moshiach, just as Moshiach will be revealed in the darkness of ikvesa dimeshicha.

title.en: The stone that falls from high

summary.en: The Rav describes the great trials of today's generation and asks whether it is lacking for being so low. With the mashal of a stone dropped into mud from a roof, he explains that today's souls fell from high and can raise sparks earlier generations could not, which is why great souls are sometimes born to simple fathers.

title.en: Chochmah, the hidden source of binah

summary.en: The Rav learns the Tanya's words that chochmah is the source of intellect and above understanding. He illustrates it with a river fed by a hidden spring, the pasuk of the river going out of Eden, an inventor who can explain his machine but not why things fall, and a pilpul whose starting point cannot itself be explained. He breaks off to continue after Chanukah, and closes by noting the yahrzeit of the Maggid, the source of all of Chassidus, with lechaim and a niggun.

catalogTitle: Current Events: Conquering the Fear of our Times With אמונה

oneLiner.en: Speaking impromptu as war with Iraq looms, the Rav explains that the troubles before Moshiach can come as fear alone, that Hashem runs events hidden as in the Megillah, and that the answer to the fear is bitachon.

abstract.en: Asked to speak about current events, the Rav begins with Chazal's chevlei Moshiach, the birth pains before the redemption, and shows they need not be harsh: Mitzrayim lasted 210 years instead of 400, and tzaddikim said the Holocaust could have been worse. The pain can come as fear alone. He explains the double hiding, hester b'soch hester, that the Torah foretells, with a mashal of a son who does not even know his father is near. The fear today comes from Yishmael, worst of the oppressors, a 'pere adam' no one can reason with. Adar, the end of the year, mirrors the end of time: its miracles, like the Megillah's, are cloaked in nature, and every event today is part of a Megillah being written. The Torah commands bitachon, and one who trusts Hashem breaks the hester panim. He closes with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, a world without clear leadership, and the strength of a double Adar.

en: The Rav explains that chevlei Moshiach need not be physical suffering; Klal Yisrael can go through them with fear alone.
Before Moshiach there is hester b'soch hester: Hashem is hidden and the hiding itself is hidden.
Like the events of the Megillah, everything happening today is part of Hashem's hidden plan to help the Jewish people.
The Torah commands bitachon, and one who relies on Hashem sees that Hashem takes care of him and breaks through the hester panim.
Real bitachon is a lifelong work that must be practiced until it becomes second nature.
Before Moshiach the Jewish people are left without leaders who can say with certainty what Hashem wants, so they must rely on Hashem alone.

title.en: Chevlei Moshiach can come as fear

summary.en: Speaking without preparation, the Rav compares the coming of Moshiach to a birth with its pains, and shows from Mitzrayim, the Rebbe Reb Elimelech and the Holocaust that the pains need not be harsh. He says the discomfort can come as fear alone, and that we seem to be in the era of ikvesa d'Meshicha.

title.en: Hester b'soch hester: the double hiding

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Vayelech that Hashem will hide His face before the end, and why tzaddikim no longer show open wonders. He explains the double hiding with a mashal of a hunter's son who does not even know his father is near, and cites the Ba'al Shem Tov's fear of this state.

title.en: The four kingdoms and Yishmael

summary.en: Turning to the looming war with Iraq, the Rav goes through the four kingdoms that oppressed the Jews since the first churban, up to Edom in which we still are, and says the Midrashim and the Rambam describe the trouble from Yishmael before Moshiach as the worst. He repeats that this trouble can come as fear.

title.en: Adar, the end of time, and hidden miracles

summary.en: The Rav explains that the year is a miniature of all time: Nisan is revealed miracles, and Adar, its end, is miracles cloaked in nature. In the Megillah Hashem's name never appears and the miracles are a chain of small incidents, yet 'the King' and even Achashveirosh allude to Hashem who directs everything.

title.en: A Megillah being written today

summary.en: With a mashal of bochurim in the days of Achashveirosh who brushed off the news about Vashti, the Rav says everything world leaders say and do today is part of a Megillah. As with Haman's decree, the trouble may stay a fear, and the fear comes from Yishmael, a 'pere adam' with whom one cannot reason, unlike earlier oppressors.

title.en: The mitzvah of bitachon

summary.en: The Rav says the answer to the fear is bitachon, a mitzvah rooted in the first of the Aseres HaDibros. One who tells Hashem that he relies on Him sees Hashem's care and breaks the hester panim, and his bitachon helps all of Klal Yisrael. He brings Shoshanas Yaakov and the Steipler sitting by his window during the Gulf War.

title.en: Practicing bitachon; a chain of rescues

summary.en: The Rav says real bitachon takes a lifetime of practice, but one must start now. He tells of a Jewish soldier saved by saying Shema, says the survivors of the Holocaust will not suffer a second such blow, and recounts how Russia fell apart just before the Gulf War, part of a chain of miracles since the Holocaust.

title.en: No leaders, no fear, and the strength of Adar

summary.en: The Rav urges not to fear but to learn, daven and give tzedakah, and explains that before Moshiach the Jews are left without leaders who can tell them Hashem's word, so they must rely on Hashem. He asks that the fear fall on the goyim as Haman's decree turned on him, and closes with the Gemara that Adar is a time of victory, doubled this year.

catalogTitle: חכמה - שורש אמונה שהוא למעלה מהשגה. פתי יאמין לכל דבר - לגבי ה' כלנו פתיים. רוב יהודים ימסרו נפשם לה' חוץ אם יש לו קשר לגוי.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains from Tanya chapter 18 that every Jew's emunah comes from chochmah, which is above understanding, so that most Jews will give their lives for Hashem, unless, as the Tzemach Tzedek notes, a connection to the goy has cut them off.

abstract.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 18: chochmah is the root of the intellect, a level that cannot be grasped, and the light of the Ein Sof is clothed in it. Since even the lowest Jewish soul contains chochmah, every Jew, even the unlearned, believes in Hashem, for emunah begins where understanding ends. He explains 'a simpleton believes everything' and says that before Hashem all are simpletons, as David HaMelech called himself a beast before Hashem and therefore always with Him. This natural bond, like an animal's devotion to its young, is why even sinners give their lives for kiddush Hashem, as the Toldos story and Jewish history show. Why only 'most'? The Tzemach Tzedek excludes one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum, because these bind a Jew to the goy. The Rav applies this at length to modern culture, media and the internet, and closes with the Torah and sefarim that keep a Jew bound to Hashem.

en: Chochmah is a level above understanding in which the light of the Ein Sof is clothed, and every Jewish soul, even the lowest, contains it.
Emunah means believing what one does not understand, so it comes from chochmah, and therefore even women who do not learn and the unlearned believe in Hashem.
Before Hashem every person is a simpleton, as David HaMelech said he was like a beast before Hashem, and through this he was always with Him.
Even the lowest Jews and sinners, for the most part, give their lives for kiddush Hashem, because a Jew is bound to his Source and cannot tear himself away.
The Tzemach Tzedek notes that one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum is an exception, because these carry a connection to the goy.
The Rav says that today the goy has entered Jewish homes through media and the internet, and this cuts a Jew off from the kedushah of Yisrael.
