title.en: Chochmah above understanding as the root of emunah

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 18 and explains that chochmah is the root of the intellect that cannot be grasped, where the light of the Ein Sof is clothed. Since every Jewish soul contains chochmah, and emunah is belief in what one does not understand, even women and the unlearned believe in Hashem.

title.en: A simpleton believes everything; before Hashem all are simpletons

summary.en: The Rav explains the passuk in Mishlei that a simpleton believes everything while the clever one understands, and compares the Jew's inborn emunah to a hen that guards her eggs with no intellect, out of natural love. He concludes that before Hashem all are simpletons, as David HaMelech said he was like a beast before Hashem and therefore always with Him.

title.en: Even sinners give their lives: the story in the Toldos

summary.en: The Rav reads that even the lowest Jews and sinners mostly give their lives for kiddush Hashem, because a Jew is bound to Hashem as a child to its parents. He tells the story brought in the Toldos, which chassidim attribute to Adel, the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter, about a thief who let himself be burned rather than convert.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh in Jewish history, and why only 'most'

summary.en: The Rav brings examples from Jewish history: the Crusades, the decrees of Tach v'Tat, and the expulsion from Spain, where whole communities died or left everything rather than convert. He then asks why the Tanya says only 'most', and why some in Spain did convert.

title.en: The Tzemach Tzedek: chametz and chalav akum

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tzemach Tzedek's note that one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum is not among those who give their lives. He explains that chametz is linked to avodah zarah and that chalav akum means having no connection to the goy, which sells a Jew to the klipah called goy; being a goy includes the goy's dress, culture and way of thinking.

title.en: The goy's hatred as a protection; the Ba'al HaTanya and Napoleon

summary.en: The Rav explains from Tehillim that Hashem turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate the Jews, and that throughout the galus the goyim's hatred and the ghettos kept Jews from mixing with them. He tells that the Ba'al HaTanya preferred Russian rule to Napoleon, who would give the Jews freedom, because that would be good materially but bad spiritually.

title.en: Infected with the goy in America today

summary.en: The Rav describes how Jews in America today take on the goy's culture through radio, television, offices, food, literature and news, and contrasts this with Jewish foods that carry kedushah. He brings the pesukim about mixing with the nations and being separated from them, and the special siman in Shulchan Aruch, and returns to chalav akum as the reason a minority will not give their lives.

title.en: Tosfos on wine touched to cause a loss

summary.en: The Rav brings a Tosfos in Avodah Zarah that wine a goy touched only to cause the Jew a loss is not yayin nesech, with the proof from a chassid who drank such wine and later gave his life for kiddush Hashem. He explains that by the Tanya's rule, his mesirus nefesh is a sign that the wine was not yayin nesech and the psak was true.

title.en: The goy in the home today, and the remedy of Torah

summary.en: The Rav says that earlier non-observant Jews had no connection to the goy, but today the goy has entered everywhere, through books, newspapers, radio and the internet, and shapes the mind as Torah would. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on lighting Chanukah candles inside, since the public domain has entered the home, and closes that Torah, sefarim and stories of tzaddikim keep a Jew bound to the chochmah of the Ein Sof and to emunah.

catalogTitle: מסירת נפש אפי' בלי דעת כי אמונה למעלה מן דעת. ברית מילה למעלה מן הדעת. ישמעאל וא”י. אהבה מסותרת. “נר ה' נשמת אדם” על פי חסידות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's emunah is above understanding, which is why even the simplest Jew gives up his life rather than deny Hashem, why bris milah is done on an eight-day-old baby, and how the soul is 'the candle of Hashem'.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 18, the Rav explains that every Jew, even the simplest, inherited emunah from the Avos and heard 'Anochi' at Har Sinai, and that this emunah is above daas: before Hashem everyone is a 'peti' who simply believes, and that is the greatest wisdom. Simple Jews who do not think about Hashem's greatness still give up their lives rather than deny Him, not out of fear of Gehinnom or hope for Gan Eden, but because the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem, just as a person cannot jump off a roof. He then brings the argument of Yishmael and Yitzchak before the Akeidah and asks why milah, the greatest mitzvah, is given to a baby who has no kavanah. His answer: milah is emunah, above daas. He adds that a goy's milah is not milah, that Eretz Yisroel is 'the Jew of geography', and links Chevron to milah and Shechem to periah. Opening chapter 19, he explains 'ner Hashem nishmas adam' through the custom of lighting a Shabbos candle for each child, and begins the image of the flame that always rises.

en: Every Jew, even the simplest, has emunah inherited from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov and implanted at Har Sinai, and this emunah is above daas.
Before Hashem every person is a 'peti' who simply believes, and believing that way is the greatest wisdom.
Simple Jews give up their lives for emunah not out of reward or punishment but because the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem.
Milah is given to an eight-day-old baby because milah is emunah, the bond with Avraham Avinu that is above daas.
A goy's milah is not considered milah, since he is entirely orlah, while a Jew has orlah only in one place.
The soul is the 'candle of Hashem', which is why many light another Shabbos candle for each child born.

title.en: Emunah above daas: everyone a 'peti'

summary.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 18, the Rav explains that every Jew inherited emunah from the Avos and heard 'Anochi' at Sinai, and that emunah is above daas. He brings 'peti ya'amin lechol davar' and 'va'ani va'ar velo eida' to show that before Hashem everyone is a simple believer, and that this is the greatest wisdom.

title.en: Why simple Jews give up their lives

summary.en: The Rav asks why simple Jews, who do not contemplate Hashem and sin in other areas, still give up their lives rather than deny Him. He answers that it is not fear of Gehinnom or hope of reward, but that the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem, just as a sane person cannot jump off a roof.

title.en: Yishmael's claim and milah without kavanah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's account of the argument between Yishmael and Yitzchak before the Akeidah. Citing the Shulchan Aruch that milah is the greatest mitzvah, and the question whether mitzvos need kavanah, he contrasts the Ba'al Shem Tov's tefillin with an ordinary person's, and asks why such a mitzvah is given to a baby who cannot have kavanah: was Yishmael right? He answers that milah is above kavanah.

title.en: Milah is emunah; a goy's milah is not milah

summary.en: The Rav explains that milah binds a Jew to Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and is therefore done on a baby to show that the bond is above daas. Yishmael's milah is merely a cut: from the Mishnah in Nedarim and the episode of Shechem he shows that a goy, even circumcised, is not called circumcised, because he is entirely orlah while a Jew has orlah in one place only.

title.en: Eretz Yisroel, Chevron and Shechem

summary.en: The Rav calls Eretz Yisroel 'the Jew of geography' and explains that milah has two parts, milah and periah: Chevron, where Avraham was circumcised, is the place of milah, and Shechem, linked to Yosef and Yehoshua, is the place of periah, which is why Yaakov's sons cut off its inhabitants. He returns to milah at eight days as emunah above daas, and describes the custom in Eretz Yisroel of saying Shema with closed eyes before a bris.

title.en: Hidden love and a candle for each child

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter 19, the Rav recalls that every Jew has a hidden love of Hashem that comes out at mesiras nefesh, and introduces 'ner Hashem nishmas adam'. He describes the widespread Ashkenazi custom of lighting two Shabbos candles from the wedding, for zachor and shamor, and adding a candle for each child, because each child is another soul, another light.

title.en: The soul as a flame that rises

summary.en: The Rav explains 'ner Hashem nishmas adam' as the Tanya does: the soul is like the light of a candle, which constantly flickers upward. He notes that fire has no solidity, yet unlike water on a slope it does not fall but rises, and leaves the question of why for the next shiur.

catalogTitle: נשמות ישראל כמו נר לאבוקה לגבי ה' הם בטלים אצלו. מכת חושך. יין של פורים. ביטול הוא מהות הקדושה וסטרא אחרא להיפוך. לחיים יא”צ הר”ר זישא.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 19, the Rav explains that the soul's longing to be nullified in Hashem like a candle in a torch comes from chochmah, the root of all kedushah, which is bittul, while the sitra achra is the opposite: self-importance even in giving.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Tanya chapter 19: like a candle flame drawn into a great torch even though it will be extinguished, every level of the soul longs to return to its Root, Hashem, the true Father who gives it every breath. This longing is beyond reason because it stems from chochmah, which cannot be grasped. He ties chochmah to the plague of darkness: there is a darkness of light too great to absorb, which is why 'borei choshech' is a higher word than 'yotzer ohr'. Purim brings down such a hidden light of chochmah, so its wine is different, just as wool becomes tzitzis. The Tanya then says all kedushah is bittul. The Rav explains true humility through Moshe Rabbeinu, signatures of 'hakatan', receiving from a Rebbe, and the Chernobyl story of the son who took 'nothing'. The sitra achra is the reverse: even its kindness, like a merchant's, seeks a return. He closes with a l'chaim for the yahrzeit of Rebbe Reb Zusha.

en: Like a candle drawn into a torch, every level of the soul longs to return to Hashem, its Root, even though it would be completely nullified there.
This longing is above reason because it comes from the chochmah of the soul, which is beyond understanding.
The plague of darkness corresponds to chochmah: a light so great that it appears as darkness, and Purim brings down a hidden light of this kind.
The rule of kedushah is bittul: whatever is holy is nullified before Hashem, and this is the true meaning of humility.
The sitra achra is the opposite: even when its people give, they give for themselves and want something back.

candidateTopics: bittul as the essence of kedushah

title.en: A candle drawn into the torch

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 19: like a candle flame drawn into a torch, every level of the soul longs to return to Hashem, the true Father, even at the cost of being nullified. He explains that this nature is above reason because it stems from the chochmah of the soul.

title.en: The plague of darkness and chochmah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the plague of darkness corresponds to chochmah: there is a darkness that is light too intense to absorb, which is why the blessing says 'borei choshech', a higher word than 'yotzer ohr'. Purim brings down such a hidden light of chochmah all day, which is why it is tied to Esther and to concealment.

title.en: Why Purim wine is different

summary.en: The Rav asks whether Purim wine is not the same wine as all year, and answers with meshalim: an esrog, wool made into tzitzis and leather made into tefillin straps become different things once holy names rest on them. Wine on an ordinary day is shown in a bad light, Kiddush and Pesach wine carry their own holy names, and Purim wine is 'yayin hameshumar', equal in gematria to Esther.

title.en: Kedushah is bittul: true humility

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's rule that all kedushah is drawn from chochmah, which is nullified before the Ein Sof. He explains that humility is not walking with a lowered head, which is really a form of pride, but being batel to Hashem like Moshe Rabbeinu, who was a king; he illustrates with the capital 'I' in English, the signature 'hakatan' of gedolim, and the small aleph of Vayikra.

title.en: Bittul before Hashem, a Rebbe and a friend

summary.en: The Rav says one who knows Shas and boasts of it has pride, and compares the boaster to a fly claiming to be bigger than another fly beside the Empire State Building. A Yid is batel to Hashem, to his friend and to his Rebbe; one can receive from a Rebbe only when one feels smaller, like a cup held below the bottle's spout.

title.en: Koach mah and the son who took nothing

summary.en: The Rav laments that today much is imitation and bittul is missing. Returning to the Tanya, he explains that chochmah is 'koach mah', from Moshe Rabbeinu's 'venachnu mah', the highest humility compared with Avraham's 'afar va'efer' and Dovid's 'tola'as'. He tells of Reb Mordechai of Chernobyl's sons, each of whom took one of his father's middos, while the youngest took his 'nothing'.

title.en: The sitra achra: giving in order to get

summary.en: The Rav reads that the sitra achra is the opposite of bittul: the nations act for themselves even in charity, for honor and a monument. He maps the seven nations of Eretz Yisroel against the seven middos, with Canaan as chesed, and explains from Rashi why a merchant is called a 'Canaani' and why 'socher' means going around in a circle: the grocer gives in order to get back. The chesed of kedushah gives without wanting anything back.

title.en: L'chaim for Rebbe Reb Zusha's yahrzeit

summary.en: The Rav notes that it is the yahrzeit of Rebbe Reb Zusha and makes a l'chaim, with an exchange about the drink and about bishul. He tells how Rebbe Reb Zusha's fear of Heaven was so great that a word of kabbalah alone would overwhelm him, and mentions the Chernobyl custom of saying Parshas Haman on the Tuesday of Beshalach.

catalogTitle: ברכת החמה: The Revelation that the Power of the Sun Belongs to יעקב

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sun, now harnessed to Esav and the order of nature, returns every 28 years to its point of origin, when it belongs to Yaakov and is blessed in Birkas HaChamah, and that this year's Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach carries great hope for the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's teaching that Yaakov and Esav are never up together, and shows it in Yerushalayim, usually spelled without its second yud while Rome stands. Hashem gave the red sun to Esav and the white moon to Yaakov, yet in truth everything was created for Yisrael; the sun is only harnessed to Esav's wagon of nature until Moshiach. Esav merely mimics Yaakov; he is a mirage, and one of his aliases is chametz, so burning chametz is destroying Amalek. The Rav then develops a law of return: everything goes back to its root, as in yovel, where a Jew returns to the fiftieth level above nature. Nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles, and the sun, king of nature, returns to its first point every 28 years; then it belongs to Yaakov and is blessed. Falling on Erev Pesach, this Birkas HaChamah signals great hopes. He closes by urging joyful acceptance of Hashem's will, even if clouds prevent the brachah.

en: Yaakov and Esav are like two sides of a seesaw: when one rises the other falls, so Hashem gave the sun to Esav and the moon to Yaakov.
In truth everything, the sun included, belongs to Yisrael; the sun is only harnessed now to Esav's wagon of nature, and when Moshiach comes both sun and moon will belong to Yaakov.
Everything in creation must return to its root; yovel is the return of a Jew to his root, the fiftieth level, which is above nature.
The sun, king of nature, returns every 28 years to the exact point where it stood at creation on the fourth day, and only then, when it belongs to Yaakov, is a brachah made over it.
Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach, the morning of burning chametz, is an especially strong return to the root, tied to the tradition that the wiping out of Amalek will be on Erev Pesach.
The Rav says a person should try to serve Hashem as best he can, but when circumstances do not follow his plan he should accept it with joy, even if clouds keep him from making the brachah.

candidateTopics: yovel and the return to the root

title.en: Yaakov and Esav on a seesaw; sun and moon

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yaakov and Esav are never up together, as Tzor filled up from the ruin of Yerushalayim, and explains why Yerushalayim is usually written without its second yud while Rome exists. He then explains that the red sun was given to Esav and the white moon to Yaakov, which is why Yisrael counts by the moon.

title.en: The sun truly belongs to Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains from Rashi that the world was created for Yisrael, so the sun too belongs to them, and is now only harnessed to Esav's wagon of nature. When Moshiach comes both lights will belong to Yaakov, who holds Esav's heel; Esav only mimics Yaakov and is in truth a mirage.

title.en: Chametz, Esav's alias

summary.en: The Rav explains that Esav has many names, one of them chametz, so burning chametz on Erev Pesach destroys Amalek. He distinguishes chametz from machmetzes, the leaven that spreads it, bringing the Or HaChaim's dream of fighting the male and female forces of evil, where the female was stronger, and contrasts the nations' 'ladies first' with the Jewish way of right over left.

title.en: The law of return and the yovel

summary.en: The Rav lays down a 'law of return': everything must go back to its root, as Koheles describes the cycle of water. He shows it in yovel, when the eved returns to his family, in Yetzias Mitzrayim as the Ramban explains, and in the fiftieth level, which is above the seven-by-seven of nature.

title.en: The sun's yovel every 28 years

summary.en: The Rav explains that nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles and the 28 letters of the Torah's first passuk, and that the sun, king of nature, returns every 28 years to the point where it was placed on the fourth day. This is the sun's yovel, and then, when it belongs to Yaakov, a brachah is made over it.

title.en: Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that when the sun's return falls on Erev Pesach it is far stronger, because of the tradition that Amalek will be wiped out on Erev Pesach and the Gemara's concern that the Beis HaMikdash may be built on Pesach. Time itself returns to its origin, the first 'time to be born', and the coming of Moshiach is a birth; he calls on every Jew to make a reckoning of how he can be reborn.

title.en: Like an infant with its mother

summary.en: The Rav brings Dovid HaMelech's comparison of himself to an infant with its mother and tells of a chassid whose Rebbe wrote 'sometimes do the opposite' beside each line of his daily schedule. He applies this to Birkas HaChamah: prepare fully, but if clouds prevent the brachah, accept it with joy, knowing that Jews around the world are saying it.

catalogTitle: יש גוי בתוך יהודי - ועל זה צריך לעשות תשובה. אצל רשעים הנפש אלקות בגלות והיא אנוס לעשות עבירה - זה גלות השכינה. בעצם חכמה אין פגם אבל בהתפשטות החכמה יש פגם וזה פוגם בחכמה ממש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 19, the Rav explains that a sinning Jew drags his G-dly soul into exile, yet the very root of its chochmah stays untouched and wakes up in a test of emunah, which is why even a sinner gives his life for kiddush Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the reading of the sefarim that 'the stranger in your midst' of the tochachah is the goy inside every Jew, and cites a student of the Ba'al Shem Tov that one must do teshuvah for it before Shabbos; he tells of a Breslover ger who would roar at night to cut the goy out of himself. Following Tanya chapter 19, he explains that the sinner submits to the yetzer hara and forces his G-dly soul into exile, which is galus haShechinah, like a captured prince forced to fight his own father. The hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu is only covered. He then resolves a contradiction: the essence of chochmah is never touched by sin, but its spreading into the heart is, and that essence sleeps until a test of emunah wakes it. He illustrates this with a story of the Czar and a Jewish soldier, and, on the yahrzeit of the Rayatz, with stories of his mesiras nefesh and his holiness.

en: The Rav explains that 'the stranger in your midst' refers to the aspect of a goy inside a Jew, and that one must do teshuvah for it before entering Shabbos.
When a Jew sins, even an otherwise upright Jew, his G-dly soul is in exile and is forced to take part in the sin; this is galus haShechinah.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, which in a sinner is covered by a garment of klipah but never lost.
The essence of chochmah in the soul is not blemished by sin; only its spreading into the heart and the whole person is.
In ordinary sins the chochmah sleeps, but a test of emunah reaches it and wakes it, so even the lowest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem.

candidateTopics: hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu

title.en: The goy within every Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings the reading of the sefarim that 'the stranger in your midst' is the goy inside a Jew, and a student of the Ba'al Shem Tov who said one must do teshuvah for it before Shabbos. He tells of a ger among the Breslover chassidim who would roar at night to cut the goy out of himself.

title.en: The G-dly soul in exile: galus haShechinah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sinner submits to the yetzer hara in the left side of the heart rather than to his G-dly soul, yet before the test of emunah of the first two commandments he gives his life. He reads the Tanya that the sinner's G-dly soul is in exile and is forced into the sin, which is galus haShechinah, and stresses this applies to any Jew when he sins.

title.en: The captive prince and the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav gives the mashal of a prince captured by his father's enemies and forced to fight against his father, and explains the Tanya's 'hidden love' through the passuk in Mishlei: an inheritance from Avraham Avinu that in a sinner is covered by klipah. He then reads that a spirit of folly enters through this covering, and that the exile reaches only the spreading of chochmah.

title.en: Essence of chochmah versus its spreading

summary.en: The Rav raises a contradiction: earlier the Tanya said sin does not reach the chochmah, yet here the sinner drags it into exile. He answers that the essence of chochmah, the emunah, cannot be touched, but its spreading into the heart and the whole body, like the sun's rays, is blemished; the root stays in the brain.

title.en: The sleeping chochmah wakes at a test of emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that during sin the chochmah in the brain sleeps, but a test of emunah, which is above reason, wakes it, so even the worst sinner refuses to separate from Hashem. He contrasts the tzaddik who rules his heart with the rasha ruled by it, and brings pesukim that before Hashem all the klipos melt away.

title.en: The Czar and the Jewish soldier

summary.en: The Rav tells a story known among Russian chassidim: a Czar in disguise drinks with a Jewish soldier who pawns his sword for drink, escapes the Czar's trap with a wooden sword, and rises to general. When ordered to convert, the soldier, who had committed every sin, leaps from a bridge into the water, and the Czar remarks that a Jew gives his life when it comes to mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Rayatz's mesiras nefesh in Soviet Russia

summary.en: Noting the yahrzeit of the Lubavitcher Rebbe Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak, the Rav tells how he kept up hidden chadarim, yeshivos, davening and mikva'os under the Communists, was arrested, and answered the commissar's revolver that he has one G-d and two worlds. He adds the Machnovker Rebbe's words that only Breslover and Lubavitcher chassidim came to him in Russia, and that hundreds of Lubavitcher chassidim were killed for their mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's granddaughter

summary.en: The Rav retells what Rabbi Shimshon Pincus heard from a granddaughter of the Chofetz Chaim: as a young woman leaving Yiddishkeit she boasted to her grandfather of telephones, radio and bombs, and he foretold flights across the Atlantic, flight to the moon and a bomb that destroys a whole city, yet she stayed as she was. He contrasts this with the Yiddishkeit the Rayatz and his chassidim kept alive in Russia through mesiras nefesh.

title.en: Stories of the young Rayatz

summary.en: The Rav tells how the young Rayatz, working as secretary for a wealthy chassid, sensed which of a dealer's vessels truly belonged to a tzaddik, lifting each twice after doing teshuvah in case a sin dulled his sense. He then tells how Reb Peretz Chaim, bending down to pick up a coin the Rebbe's son had dropped while juggling by a window, escaped a Communist's bullet, and the shiur ends with l'chaim.

catalogTitle: כל עבירה היא ע”ז ממש והעובר הוא יותר גרוע מהסטרא אחרא ממש. הסטרא אחרא נהנה מבחינת אחוריים. אם חוטא' יתוש קדמך. תרץ למה אין כל עבירה דוחה פיקוח נפש אם כל עבירה היא ע”ז ממש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 24, the Rav explains that every sin, even a small one, is truly avodah zarah, that the sinner is lower than the sitra achra itself and even than a gnat, and why pikuach nefesh nevertheless overrides most sins.

abstract.en: The Rav announces he will now learn faster, recalls chapter 23 (anochi as the root of all mitzvos, lo yihyeh of all sins), and opens chapter 24: just as Torah and mitzvos unite a Jew with Hashem, a sin unites him with the sitra achra. Every sin is avodah zarah because the sinner makes himself a yesh who will not be batel to Hashem's will, like chametz that rises against humble matzah. He uses the very G-dly soul that animates him to power the sin, lending the sitra achra a body. The sitra achra still knows its Master and does His will; the sinner does not. It lives only from the outermost 'back' of holiness, the dregs that cannot be refined. A person sins only through a spirit of folly that hides the truth from his chochmah. Like the gnat that only takes and never gives, the sinner is lower than all creatures, and animals rule a man only when he loses his tzelem Elokim, with stories of tzaddikim and beasts. Finally the Rav asks why pikuach nefesh overrides ordinary sins and answers from the Gemara and as a gezeiras hakasuv.

en: Every sin, even a rabbinic one, is truly avodah zarah, because the sinner detaches himself from bittul to Hashem and binds himself to the sitra achra.
A sin is a yesh, a self that will not be batel to Hashem's will, and the yesh itself is avodah zarah, as chametz rises while matzah stays low.
When sinning, a Jew harnesses his G-dly soul, which gives his body life, to the sitra achra, and lends it a body with which to sin.
The sitra achra itself recognizes its Master and carries out His will, so a person who sins is worse than it.
A person sins only because a spirit of folly covers his chochmah; were it uncovered, he would give his life rather than sin, as he would for avodah zarah.
Pikuach nefesh overrides other sins not because they are lighter than avodah zarah but because of the Gemara's reasoning and a decree of the Torah.

title.en: Faster pace; review of chapter 23

summary.en: The Rav says he will now learn faster, just to know what the text says, so as to reach the later chapters. He recalls chapter 23: anochi is the root of all mitzvos and lo yihyeh of all sins, so every sin is avodah zarah, and asks why a person who would give his life rather than worship idols does not make the same calculation for every sin.

title.en: A sin as union with the sitra achra

summary.en: Opening chapter 24, the Rav explains that just as Torah study unites a person with Hashem, a sin unites him with the sitra achra. The sinner is a yesh who will not be batel, and a yesh is avodah zarah; he illustrates with chametz, which rises, against matzah, which stays low, and with haughtiness.

title.en: The G-dly soul harnessed to the sin

summary.en: The Rav explains that through thought, speech and action of a sin the soul itself is united with avodah zarah: the G-dly soul that animates the body is made into a horse pulling the wagon of the sin, and the sinner lends the sitra achra a body. He adds that the sitra achra knows its Master and does His will, so the sinner is worse than it.

title.en: The sitra achra lives from the 'back'

summary.en: The Rav explains that even idol-worshippers call Hashem the G-d of gods and believe He handed the world to lesser powers; their sin is that they consider themselves a yesh. Everything must draw some life from holiness, and the sitra achra draws only from the 'back', the part that cannot be refined, like the waste of food; the sinner, who goes against Hashem's will, is worse.

title.en: Dregs of this world and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Rav explains that the evil of this material world is the dregs of the kelipos, like the sediment of spoiled wine, which is why the wicked are strong here. He brings the Gemara that a person sins only when a spirit of folly enters him, and explains why the woman of the parsha of sotah would give her life rather than bow to an idol yet commits a sin: the folly covers her chochmah, which is roused only by real avodah zarah.

title.en: Even the gnat preceded you

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a gnat was created before man and explains it: every creature both receives from the world and gives to it, like the bee, but the gnat only sucks blood and gives nothing, the very mark of the sitra achra. Yet a sinner, who goes against Hashem's will, is lower still; he tells of a tzaddik who would not kill any creature except a mosquito.

title.en: Beasts and the tzelem Elokim: stories

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that a wild beast rules over a man only when he looks to it like an animal, having lost his tzelem Elokim. He tells how lions bowed before the Divrei Chaim, how a pack of wolves left a family of the Komarna Rebbe's descendants unharmed, and of a gadol who saw a leader without a tzelem Elokim; and he mentions Daniel among the lions.

title.en: Why pikuach nefesh overrides other sins

summary.en: The Rav asks: if every sin is avodah zarah, why does pikuach nefesh override all sins but avodah zarah? He answers with the Gemara's reasoning, desecrate one Shabbos so he can keep many, and that it is a gezeiras hakasuv, not because Shabbos is lighter; he shows from the law of shechitah that a mumar for Shabbos is like an idolater. He closes with a word about the coming week.

catalogTitle: Marriage: Giving the Ring - A Symbol of the Essence of Marriage

oneLiner.en: Speaking to a chassan and kallah during their sheva brachos, the Rav explains that marriage, like Shabbos the bride of Knesses Yisrael, is built on giving, and that the ring of kiddushin is the first act of that giving.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Adam and Chava, created as one and then separated, and explains that every chassan finds the kallah he was once one with. Shabbos too is a bride: Hashem gave her Knesses Yisrael as her partner, and since Shabbos is pure neshamah, souls can unite with her. The seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's own Shabbos, and the seventh bracha unites the chassan and kallah with Yerushalayim, the bereaved kallah. Turning to kiddushin, he asks why Beis Hillel allows a mere perutah, and answers that kiddushin is the start of a life of giving: what counts is not what one gives but how, with respect. Nesuin itself means giving. The kallah, silent and passive, gives the greatest gift, herself, just as Shabbos seems to take yet gives all brachos. He brings the Rambam's directions for husband and wife, describes how mutual giving builds happiness, and closes by urging the couple to learn their two heritages together, reading from Rav Hirsch on Shabbos.

en: Every chassan and kallah were one in Adam and Chava, and Hashem reunites them in one house.
Shabbos is the kallah of Knesses Yisrael, and the seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's own Shabbos.
Kiddushin is the first act of giving, and what counts is not how much one gives but how, with respect.
Nesuin means giving: the husband commits himself to give all his life without thinking of taking.
The kallah's silent passivity at kiddushin is the highest giving: she gives her very self.
Following the Rambam's directions, each spouse's giving draws out the other's, and that is the secret of a happy home.

candidateTopics: Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on kiddushin
the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch

title.en: Adam, Chava and Shabbos the bride

summary.en: The Rav describes Adam and Chava, created as one person and then separated, as the roots of every chassan and kallah. He then brings the Midrash that Shabbos complained it had no partner and was given Knesses Yisrael, so that the Jewish people are joined to Shabbos and separated from it each week.

title.en: The seven days as the couple's Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav asks how human beings can be wed to Shabbos, a unit of time, and answers that Shabbos is pure neshamah, the soul of Knesses Yisrael. He explains that the seven days of sheva brachos are a private Shabbos given to the chassan and kallah, with song, rest and seven brachos, and that the seventh day is a double Shabbos.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the waiting kallah

summary.en: The Rav describes Yerushalayim as a kallah with a heavy heart, waiting for the redemption, and explains that the sheva brachos give her her own bracha before the bracha for the new chassan and kallah. The seventh bracha, the Shabbos of the brachos, unites them all, as they will all be united in the day that is entirely Shabbos.

title.en: Dinar or perutah: what kiddushin is

summary.en: Turning to the moment of kiddushin, the Rav brings the dispute of Beis Shammai, who require a dinar for the dignity of a Jewish daughter, and Beis Hillel, who allow a perutah, and asks why Beis Hillel would disagree. He rejects seeing kiddushin as a purchase and brings an essay that a person is perfect when he gives, and that a marriage succeeds only while both are conscious that they married in order to give.

title.en: Not what he gives but how

summary.en: The Rav explains that kiddushin opens married life with an act of giving. Beis Shammai want the giving to cost, while Beis Hillel teach that it is not what one gives but how: a perutah given with the awareness that the kallah is Shabbos and Yerushalayim is worth more than all treasures. The kesubah's promise of respect and the word nesuin, which he reads as giving, carry the same idea.

title.en: The kallah gives herself

summary.en: The Rav asks why the kallah gives nothing and says nothing at kiddushin, and explains that by making herself passive she gives her very self, the highest giving. To the question whether this is slavery he answers from Shabbos, which seems only to take yet is the source of all brachos, and explains that a woman, bound to the Shechinah, can give in a way a man cannot; Jewishness itself comes from the mother.

title.en: The Rambam's plan for a happy home

summary.en: Answering those who oppose this view, the Rav reads the Rambam in Hilchos Ishus: the husband honors his wife more than himself, provides for her and comes home cheerfully, and the wife honors her husband greatly. He explains that each side's giving naturally draws out the other's, and that those who seek to 'liberate' the woman destroy the structure of the family.

title.en: Two heritages: the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rav Hirsch

summary.en: The Rav turns to the chassan and kallah, descendants of a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov and of Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, and describes what each brought: the Ba'al Shem Tov to Eastern European Jewry and Rav Hirsch to Western European Jewry. He suggests that they learn together each day from both heritages, to strengthen them against outside influences and continue both golden chains.

title.en: Rav Hirsch on Shabbos, and a brachah

summary.en: To start their learning, the Rav reads a passage of Rav Hirsch describing Shabbos as the Jew's richest jewel and most loyal companion. He blesses the new couple to treasure Shabbos as their purest diamond and to fill their weekdays with avodas Hashem according to their ancestors' teachings.

catalogTitle: אין אדם חוטא אלא אם נכנס בו רוח שטות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew sins only because a spirit of folly makes him forget that every sin cuts him off from Hashem just as idolatry does, and that the same readiness for mesirus nefesh he would show against idolatry can carry him through every daily battle with the yetzer hara.

abstract.en: Learning Tanya chapter 25, the Rav recalls that even the simplest Jews gave their lives rather than worship idols in the persecutions of Europe, and teaches that every sin is a branch of idolatry, since it too separates a person from Hashem. A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly, as the Gemara says, makes him forget this; his hidden love for Hashem is always there. Even the plan to sin and then repent does not help, since the bond with Hashem is above time and even one moment of separation counts. The Rav applies the reckoning to the daily war: getting up to daven, learning with clarity and full strength, davening with kavanah, giving tzedakah. He adds that a mitzvah creates an eternal union, warns about wasted time, and cautions that today's weaker generations must also guard their health. He closes with Rashi's reading that going against one's will is itself mesirus nefesh, and explains why the generation in the desert also needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh.

en: Every sin, even a light one, is a branch of idolatry, because it too separates a Jew from Hashem.
A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly enters him and he forgets that the sin cuts him off from Hashem; his hidden love stays intact.
The bond with Hashem is above time, so even a single moment of separation is real separation, and the plan to sin and repent later changes nothing.
The same reckoning of mesirus nefesh should be used against the yetzer hara in getting up to daven, learning Torah with clarity and full strength, davening with kavanah and giving tzedakah.
A mitzvah or Torah learning creates a union with Hashem that is eternal, while time spent on idle things loses that union.
Today's generations are weaker than in the Ba'al HaTanya's time, so a person must also look after his health, as long as most of the day is given to Torah and avodah.
Going against one's own will is itself a form of mesirus nefesh, and the readiness to give one's life should be applied to all the mitzvos.

candidateTopics: every sin as a branch of idolatry

title.en: Every Jew gives his life against idolatry

summary.en: The Rav recalls that in the decrees and persecutions of Europe hundreds of thousands of simple Jews gave their lives rather than convert, and explains that every sin, even a light one, is a branch of idolatry. He says a person must sit and think about this again and again until it becomes part of his own knowledge.

title.en: The spirit of folly and the plan to repent later

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a person sins only when a spirit of folly enters him: he forgets that the sin separates him from Hashem, while his hidden love, which includes fear, remains. He then shows that even one who plans to repent afterwards would still give his life rather than bow to an idol even for a moment, because the bond with Hashem is above time.

title.en: Using the reckoning in daily avodah

summary.en: The Rav applies the reckoning to the yetzer hara's daily tricks: the laziness to get up and daven in the morning, learning without clarity and full strength, davening without kavanah, and holding back from giving tzedakah. Even for one minute, he says, a Jew would give his life rather than be cut off, so he can overcome these smaller tests.

title.en: The eternal union of a mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a mitzvah done with all one's strength makes a union with Hashem that lasts forever, since above everything is eternal and the Torah never changes. Time wasted on idle talk and things that have nothing to do with Torah or avodah loses that union, and one must then ask Hashem's forgiveness.

title.en: Weaker generations and guarding health

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Ba'al HaTanya demanded unbroken Torah and avodah of people stronger than today's, and that those who strain too much break down. A person must rest, eat properly and exercise for his health, which is not bittul Torah, as long as most of the day is given to Torah and avodah and he does not indulge in foolishness.

title.en: Selach lanu and the meaning of nafsheichem

summary.en: The Rav asks why Chazal instituted the brachah of Selach lanu three times a day, and answers that it is for bittul Torah, which the daily tamid offering used to atone for and which the tefillos now replace. He then brings Rashi that nefesh means will, so that anyone who acts against his will has a measure of mesirus nefesh.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh in Shema and in the desert

summary.en: The Rav explains that when saying Shema one must have in mind readiness for mesirus nefesh at the word echad and at bechol nafshecha. He asks why the generation in the desert, whom Hashem promised the nations would fear, needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh, and answers that it let them make the reckoning for every mitzvah and every small sin.

catalogTitle: היצר מנצח כשאדם בעצבות' קשר עצבות לעצלות. בכל עצב יהיה מותר. עצה להיות בשמחה אפ' כשבאות צרות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 26, the Rav explains why sadness lets the yetzer hara win, how a set time of broken-heartedness leads to a greater joy, and why sadness that comes in the middle of business or avodah is a trick of the yetzer.

abstract.en: The Rav learns the opening of Tanya chapter 26: just as a sluggish wrestler loses even to a weaker opponent, a person in sadness cannot defeat the yetzer, because sadness and laziness both come from the element of earth. One must be joyful, free of worry about the future and of dissatisfaction with the present. He then explains the verse 'in every sadness there is an advantage': a broken heart at a set time, as in the Arizal's order of Tikkun Chatzos followed by Tehillim 51, leads to a joy greater than before, like light after darkness. Along the way he discusses the four tefillos and four Shabbos meals, staying awake on leil shishi and Shavuos night, and the hidden chassadim that come clothed in suffering. He closes with the Tanya's warning that sadness during business or davening is a ploy of the yetzer, which leads to cravings.

en: Like a sluggish wrestler who loses to a weaker opponent, a person in sadness and heaviness cannot overcome the yetzer hara.
Sadness and laziness come from the same element of earth; a sad person lacks the joy of life and moves slowly, while zerizus comes from joy.
'In every sadness there is an advantage': the joy that comes after a true broken heart at a set time is greater, like light that comes after darkness.
Regret over one's avodah belongs only at a fixed time, such as after Tikkun Chatzos or at Krias Shema before sleep, not all day.
Suffering that comes from the hidden world is a greater kindness, and great tzaddikim rejoiced in suffering because it bound them to Hashem.
Sadness about one's spiritual standing that falls on a person in the middle of business or davening comes from the yetzer hara, which uses it to lead him to cravings.

candidateTopics: in every sadness there is an advantage
four tefillos and four Shabbos meals

title.en: Sadness and laziness lose the battle

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter 26 and its mashal of two wrestlers, adding the example of the lion and the ox. He explains that sadness and laziness both come from the element of earth, so a depressed person moves slowly and cannot defeat the yetzer.

title.en: Joy, zerizus and waking up early

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's call to be free of worry and sadness, distinguishing worry about the future from dissatisfaction with the present. He shows that people who wake up late are escaping life, while on a day they expect something good they rise early, as a Jew who looks forward to serving Hashem does.

title.en: In every sadness there is an advantage

summary.en: The Rav brings the verse 'in every sadness there is an advantage' and explains with the Tanya that the advantage is the joy that follows true regret over one's avodah. A broken heart breaks the sitra achra and the wall between a person and Hashem, as the verse 'the offerings of G-d are a broken spirit' teaches.

title.en: A set time for sadness: Tikkun Chatzos

summary.en: The Rav explains that sadness may enter only at an appointed time, for a few minutes. He shows this in the Arizal's order to say Tehillim 51, Dovid HaMelech's chapter of teshuvah, after Tikkun Chatzos, where one mourns the destruction of his own inner Beis HaMikdash and then learns in joy.

title.en: Four tefillos, four meals, and leil shishi

summary.en: The Rav digresses to the four tefillos: Shacharis and Mincha are obligations, Maariv was a choice that Jews accepted like a vow, and Dovid HaMelech's midnight tefillah remained for tzaddikim. He parallels them to the four Shabbos meals, and criticizes staying up on Thursday night only to sleep through Shabbos.

title.en: Shavuos night and serving with sense

summary.en: The Rav explains that staying awake on Shavuos night is meant to prepare for the morning, so one who will doze through davening and Kerias HaTorah gains nothing, like a chasan who arranged everything and then went to sleep at the chuppah. Since the generations have weakened, one must serve Hashem with sense, and on Shabbos rise early, learn and daven with strength.

title.en: Light after darkness; sorrows of this world

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav explains with 'as light excels over darkness' that joy after sadness is greater, and brings the Arizal's reading of 'because you did not serve Hashem with joy'. He lists other set times for a reckoning, then turns to sadness over children, health and livelihood, which the Tanya rejects, since one blesses Hashem for bad as for good.

title.en: Hidden chassadim clothed in suffering

summary.en: The Rav explains that rejoicing in suffering is a high level reached through years of work. The first two letters of Hashem's name stand for the hidden worlds, whose greater chassadim come down covered in suffering, as he shows in the word 'mitzvah', and he brings 'fortunate is the man whom Hashem chastises' and Chazal on those who rejoice in suffering.

title.en: Tzaddikim who rejoiced in suffering

summary.en: The Rav tells of tzaddikim who rejoiced in suffering, including a Rav named Eliyahu who put his hand into fire, because closeness to Hashem is better than life. He explains that the hidden chassadim will one day be revealed like the sun leaving its sheath, and that in worldly troubles one should bind himself to Hashem.

title.en: Sadness in business and avodah is the yetzer

summary.en: The Rav says simpler people should meet worldly troubles with bitachon. He then brings the Tanya that even sadness over spiritual matters, when it comes during business or davening, is a trick of the yetzer that leads to cravings, as seen in people who overeat, and that true bitterness belongs only at a fixed time such as chatzos or Krias Shema before sleep.

catalogTitle: חילוק בין עצבות ומרירות. כשמחשבות רעות באות - אז יש אפשרות לקיים מצוות ולא תתורו. שני מטעמים שהשכינה נהנות מהם. לחיים יא”צ.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 27, the Rav explains that a bad thought pushed away is not a reason for sadness but a chance to fulfill 'velo sasuru', and that the beinoni's struggle with his yetzer gives Hashem a nachas ruach of its own.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by distinguishing atzvus (dejection that makes a person withdraw and sleep) from merirus (bitterness that drives him to act), and two sources of atzvus: sins and worldly troubles. Turning to Tanya chapter 27, he explains that a person troubled by bad thoughts should not see them as a sign of distance from Hashem: pushing them out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', which speaks to beinonim, not tzaddikim. With the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that the sin lies only in letting the thought stay. In a long digression he explains that the Torah speaks to every Jew on his level, with examples of pride, anger, 'vachai bahem' and Korach. He then brings the Zohar on the nachas ruach when the sitra achra is subdued, the two kinds of 'matamim', 'leyom ra'ah', iskafya in permitted things such as delaying a meal, and 'kadesh atzmecha'. He closes with a lechayim for the yahrzeit of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz and two stories about him.

en: Atzvus is dejection that makes a person withdraw from life, while merirus is bitterness that pushes him to act; the Rav says atzvus must be avoided.
A bad thought that enters a person's mind is no sign of distance from Hashem; pushing it out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', and he should rejoice in it.
The sin is not that the thought came, but letting it stay and following it; the mitzvah is to drive it out.
When a beinoni subdues the sitra achra, Hashem has a great nachas ruach, a different kind from the nachas of tzaddikim who nullify it entirely.
Iskafya applies even in permitted things, such as holding back from eating for a while when one is hungry, and a little sanctification below brings great kedushah from above.

title.en: Atzvus versus merirus

summary.en: The Rav defines atzvus as dejection that makes a person sleep and avoid reality, and merirus as bitterness that drives him to act. He distinguishes atzvus over sins from atzvus over worldly troubles such as business, children and health.

title.en: Bad thoughts as a chance for a mitzvah

summary.en: Reading Tanya chapter 27, the Rav explains that a person who is pained by bad thoughts, thinking they show he is far from Hashem, is mistaken: when he pushes them away he fulfills 'velo sasuru acharei levavchem'. He asks whether one should then want such thoughts, and begins to answer that the pasuk does not speak to tzaddikim.

title.en: The beinoni's mitzvah of driving thoughts out

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'velo sasuru' speaks to beinonim, each with his own nisyonos, and brings Chazal that one who refrains from a sin that came his way is rewarded as for a mitzvah. With the Bnei Yissaschar he shows the sin is only in keeping the thought, calls distress over such thoughts a form of gasus haruach, and says pushing them out is a person's avodah.

title.en: The Torah speaks to each Jew on his level

summary.en: Pausing to explain the Tanya's claim that the pasuk does not speak to tzaddikim, the Rav says every word of the Torah concerns every Jew: pshat binds everyone, while great tzaddikim keep the Torah on deeper levels. He illustrates with pride and anger, 'vachai bahem', Korach's subtle jealousy, and Moshe's sin at Mei Merivah.

title.en: Subduing the sitra achra raises Hashem's glory

summary.en: Back to the Tanya, the Rav gives the example of a person in the street who remembers not to look and does not look: his mitzvah rises above and the sitra achra is knocked down. He brings the Zohar on the great nachas ruach when the sitra achra is subdued, and says a person plagued all his life by such thoughts should not be broken, since this may be why his soul came down.

title.en: Why a beinoni is created, and two kinds of nachas

summary.en: The Rav recalls the question from Tanya chapter 1 on free choice and explains the answer here: a beinoni is created to fight the sitra achra without nullifying it, and his war brings a second kind of nachas ruach beside that of tzaddikim. He connects this to the plural 'matamim' of Yitzchak and Rivkah.

title.en: Sweet and sharp delicacies; iskafya in permitted things

summary.en: The Rav compares the two kinds of nachas ruach to sweet dishes and sharp ones like horseradish made tasty with fish. He reads 'vegam rasha leyom ra'ah' as making day out of the bad, and explains that iskafya applies even in permitted things, such as delaying a meal for a while when one is hungry.

title.en: A little sanctity below, much from above

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara on the hours when people and talmidei chachamim eat, explaining that the talmid chacham waited to subdue his yetzer, and extends this to holding back from idle talk. He explains that even a little iskafya draws great kedushah from above, citing 'adam mekadesh atzmo me'at' and 'kadesh atzmecha bemutar lach', and the Tanya that true kedushah comes only through subduing the sitra achra.

title.en: Lechayim for the Ropshitzer's yahrzeit

summary.en: The Rav calls for a lechayim for the yahrzeit of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz and tells of him: a man who wore sackcloth with his shirt open so it would be seen, of whom the Ropshitzer said the Satan had caught him in the sack, and the Ropshitzer's own last words about the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: Summer: Preparing for a Good Summer (Connection to שלח/קרח and תמוז/אב)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Tammuz and Av, the months of Reuven and Shimon that fell through Korach's machlokes and the sins of their nesi'im, hide the deepest sparks of Moshiach, so a summer journey is a shlichus from Hashem to be guarded and used.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Zohar that Korach's machlokes was against Shabbos and Yerushalayim, the place of unity, and that Korach wanted the Middas HaDin to rule. Following Rashi, he explains that the world was first meant to be run with din and will be so in the future. Reuven, the firstborn whose stone is the red ruby, is din, so his tribe joined Korach. The months follow the order of the degalim: Tammuz belongs to Reuven and Av to Shimon, and because their nesi'im, Elitzur and Shlumiel, defiled themselves, these became months of churban, yet in the end they will turn to joy. Since the holiest sparks fall lowest, Tammuz and Av hold the most precious sparks of Moshiach. Every journey is a shlichus from Hashem, as the meraglim traveled in these months, so summer is no time for leniency: one must guard one's eyes, daven, and see Hashem in His creation.

en: Korach wanted the Middas HaDin to rule the world, and the Rav explains through Rashi that the world was originally meant to be run with din and will be so in the future.
Tammuz and Av are the months of Reuven and Shimon, fourth and fifth in the degalim, and the sins of their nesi'im made them months of churban.
In the future Tammuz and Av will be restored and become the happiest months of the year, as Zechariah foretells.
Because the holiest sparks fall the lowest, Tammuz and Av hold the most precious sparks of Moshiach, and these months are a special time to work to bring him.
Wherever a person travels he is a shaliach of Hashem, and he must ask himself whether he goes as a shaliach of Hashem or of the yetzer hara.
Summer is not a time to be lenient but a time of danger and trials, when one must especially guard the eyes, since Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes.
In the country one can see Hashem in His creation, which sings to Him, and a Jew is meant to join that song.

title.en: Korach's machlokes and the Middas HaDin

summary.en: The Rav announces ideas for the coming summer months and brings the Zohar, cited by the Chasam Sofer and the Maor VaShemesh, that Korach's machlokes was against Shabbos and Yerushalayim, the place of unity. Korach, a Levi, wanted din instead of the kehunah's chesed to be the order of the world.

title.en: The world was meant for din

summary.en: To simplify the Zohar, the Rav brings Rashi at the start of Bereishis that Hashem first intended to run the world with din, and added rachamim only because the world could not stand it. In the future, he explains, the Jews will be such tzaddikim that they can live and be happy even with din.

title.en: Why Reuven joined Korach

summary.en: The Rav asks why Dasan, Aviram, On and the tribe of Reuven joined Korach. He answers that Reuven, the bechor, is din, like 'reishis' and the name Elokim at creation; the firstborn lost the avodah to the Leviim after the Egel and wanted it back; and Reuven's stone on the Choshen is the red odem, called ruby or rubin, the color of pure din.

title.en: Reuven, Shimon, Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Rav explains the two orders of the shevatim: Reuven first as bechor with Shimon as his viceroy, the Choshen by birth, but in the degalim Reuven is demoted to fourth and Yehuda is first. Since the months match the shevatim of the degalim, Nissan is Yehuda's, Tammuz is Reuven's and Av is Shimon's, and Tammuz is entirely a month of din, as the Bnei Yissaschar says.

title.en: The nesi'im who brought churban

summary.en: Elitzur ben Shedeur, nasi of Reuven, joined Korach's machlokes and dragged his month, Tammuz, into churban; Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, nasi of Shimon, sinned and was killed by Pinchas, and Av became a month of churban. In the future both months will be restored, and as Zechariah says, their fasts will become days of joy.

title.en: Korach's tikkun and Monday's song

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that the last letters of 'Tzaddik katamar yifrach' spell Korach, who will come to his tikkun. Machlokes was created on Monday, the second day, when there is no 'ki tov'; therefore on Monday the song of the sons of Korach, which praises Yerushalayim, is sung.

title.en: Sparks of Moshiach in Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tammuz and Av are months of Moshiach: the Midrash says Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av. Every Jew holds a spark of Moshiach, as the Meor Einayim teaches, and sparks are captive in food, drink and every place; since the holiest fall lowest, as the Tanya explains, these fallen months hold the most precious ones.

title.en: Every journey is a shlichus

summary.en: Against Elitzur and Shlumiel the Rav sets Yehoshua and Kalev, whose tribes bring Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid and whose months, Tishrei and Nissan, are months of geulah. Then, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a man's steps are set by Hashem, he explains that every trip, to Chicago or to the country, is a shlichus to raise sparks, and that the meraglim traveled in Tammuz and Av as shluchim whose intentions decided their fate.

title.en: Whose shaliach am I

summary.en: The Rav says one who packs for vacation must ask whether he is a shaliach of Hashem or of the yetzer hara. Everything happens in place and time, as the law of edim zomemin shows, and Hashem sends a Jew into Tammuz and Av as a time of danger, so he must daven as Moshe davened for Yehoshua and Kalev davened for himself. He contrasts the failed meraglim with the successful shluchim of Yehoshua, who raised Rachav until she married Yehoshua.

title.en: Summer is no time for leniency

summary.en: The Rav warns that a yeshiva's summer break is not a release from the winter's bonds and not a time to be lenient in tznius, kashrus or Shabbos; it is a time of danger, full of the trials of ikvesa d'Meshicha, including the electronic yetzer hara. Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, so one must especially guard the eyes.

title.en: Seeing Hashem in the countryside

summary.en: The Rav says the task of Tammuz and Av is to restore them, and with them Reuven, Shimon and one's own soul. In the city one sees only cement and buildings, but in the country one sees Hashem's creation, the trees, birds, streams and stars, as Yeshayahu says to lift the eyes and look.

title.en: Singing with creation, and a blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains why morning is called tzafra, for the birds, and evening ramsha, for the insects, while a Jew sings by day and by night. He brings Rav Hirsch on 'Kol Hashem behadar' and tells how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz answered a man who told him to look in his siddur. He closes that a Jew must know whose shaliach he is, and blesses the listeners with a successful summer.

catalogTitle: תפילה היא מלחמה גדולה' זוכים לבא בהיכלות התיבות ע”י שמחה ויגיעה. מלחמת הגוף והנשמה כל ימי חייו. טעם שהמחשבות רעות בואת דוקא כשעוסקים בעבודת ה'. כלל גדול בעבודת ה' - “אין עוד מלבדו”. לחיים יא”צ ר' שלומקע זווילער זצוקללה”ה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 28, the Rav explains that foreign thoughts during davening are part of the lifelong war between the two souls, and that the way to win is to dismiss them as nothing, with joy and the great rule 'ein od milvado'.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 28 by calling davening a great war: each word of tefillah is a heichal (chamber) above, and a foreign thought is a sign that one is being kept out of it, much as the cherubim guarded Gan Eden. The Tanya says not to sink into sadness but to push in. He explains that a thought is a complete spiritual entity, so a tzaddik can elevate foreign thoughts that come to him from others, but a person whose thoughts are his own must not try. Rather he should strengthen himself with joy, knowing the thought comes from the klipah fighting the G-dly soul; it attacks precisely when one strengthens himself in avodah. Because a person has two souls, such thoughts do not show that his davening is worthless. The answer is bittul: treating them as nothing, by the great rule 'ein od milvado'. He closes with the yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil and stories about him.

en: Each word of davening is a heichal above; a foreign thought during tefillah means one is being held back from entering it.
Elevating foreign thoughts is only for tzaddikim, whose foreign thoughts come from others; a person whose thoughts are his own must not engage with them.
One must not fall into sadness over such thoughts, but strengthen himself all the more in davening with joy.
The foreign thought comes from the klipah fighting the G-dly soul in the beinoni, a lifelong war in which each side strengthens itself when the other does.
Because a person has two souls, foreign thoughts in davening are not a sign that his davening is worthless.
The way to deal with them is bittul: to treat them as nothing, by the great rule 'ein od milvado', that besides Hashem everything is nothing.

title.en: Davening as a war for the heichalos

summary.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 28 and explains that each word of davening is a heichal; angels keep a person out with foreign thoughts, like the cherubim at Gan Eden. The Tanya says not to be sad but to push one's way in, as chassidim used to.

title.en: Elevating thoughts: only for tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav explains that every thought is a complete spiritual entity, sometimes a soul seeking a tikkun, which a tzaddik elevates to love or fear of Hashem. The Tanya warns that this is only for tzaddikim, whose foreign thoughts are not their own; someone whose thoughts are his own cannot elevate them.

title.en: No sadness: the klipah's war

summary.en: The Rav says a person must not despair and cry out over his thoughts, but strengthen himself with joy in davening. The thought comes from the klipah in the left chamber of the heart, which wages a lifelong war with the G-dly soul, like two wrestlers.

title.en: Why the thoughts come during avodah

summary.en: The Rav asks why bad thoughts come precisely when a person davens or resolves to improve, and answers that when the side of holiness strengthens itself, the other side fights back harder. He rejects the conclusion that such thoughts prove one is worthless.

title.en: Two souls, and the parable of the distracter

summary.en: The Rav explains that if a person had only one soul, a thought during davening would show something is wrong; but since he has two, the animal soul's thoughts say nothing about the davening. He brings the Tanya's parable of one who speaks with a friend while a wicked man stands opposite trying to distract him.

title.en: Bittul: 'you are nothing'

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the way to deal with foreign thoughts is to nullify them, treating them as utterly nothing, like something dead. He tells stories of tzaddikim on this theme, much of which the recording leaves unclear.

title.en: The great rule: ein od milvado

summary.en: The Rav calls 'ein od milvado' a great rule in avodas Hashem: one who remembers that everything besides Hashem is nothing can win all his battles. One does not enter into conversation with the distracter, but strengthens himself in his kavanah.

title.en: The fly, and asking for mercy

summary.en: After a remark about the end of the Sefirah period, the Rav brings that one of the yetzer hara's names is a fly, which keeps coming back however often it is chased away. When a thought will not leave, the Tanya's advice is to pour out one's heart to Hashem and ask for mercy on the G-dly soul.

title.en: Yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil

summary.en: The Rav marks the yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil and tells how he said the gates of teshuvah would open before Moshiach, and how at the Kosel he pointed out houses that would be torn down, as happened in the Six Day War. He closes with l'chaim and wishes for yeshuos for Klal Yisroel.

catalogTitle: היום לא כל כך שכיח עתות רצון בשעת התפילה כי אוכלים מאכלות אסורות ויש טימטום הלב. עצה - לשבר את הגוף אבל רק בעתות מזומנים. כל אדם מעריך גופו כעיקר והנשמה כנטפל לו' אבל בצדיקים בהיפך.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 29, the Rav explains why the heart can become as dull as stone, why this is so common today, and how one breaks the coarseness of the body so the light of the neshamah can take hold in it.

abstract.en: After opening words on the days of tashlumim after Shavuos, accepting the yoke of Heaven, and preparing all week for Shabbos, the Rav reads Tanya chapter 29 on timtum halev, the heart that becomes like stone. He links it to the Gemara's reading of 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem': forbidden food blocks the heart, and he explains why kashrus today demands great care. A long digression on the taste and light that holiness puts into Shabbos follows, with stories of Kuzmir, the Satmar Rav and the Lechovitcher rebbetzin. Back in Tanya, he brings the Zohar's advice: wood that will not catch fire is chopped, so the body is broken at set times with a ruach nishbarah. He contrasts the beinoni, whose self is the body, with the tzaddik, whose self is the soul, explains Dovid's 'I am a worm and not a man', and ends with how to rebuke the body, through the story of a ger tzedek.

en: The Rav explains that timtum halev, a dull heart that feels no joy in learning or davening, can come from forbidden food, as the Gemara reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem'.
He says this is common today because packaged food with countless ingredients and lesser hechsherim make kashrus hard, unlike the Ba'al HaTanya's time when food was cooked at home.
The Tanya's advice, from the Zohar, is to break the body: like wood that will not catch fire, it must be chopped so the light of the soul can take hold.
The body blocks the soul because of its coarseness, which comes from the strength of kelipas nogah, the animal soul that gives the body life.
In a beinoni the self is the body and the soul is something added to him, while in a tzaddik the soul is the person and the body is only his garment.
The Rav says one must speak to the body and the yetzer hara and rebuke its chutzpah for rising over the neshamah and taking away the sweetness of Torah.

title.en: After Shavuos, before Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav opens with the seven days after Shavuos in which one can still make up the yom tov and take one's share in Torah, speaks of accepting the yoke of Heaven in a time of danger and of the protection Hashem gives through Sukkos, and then of preparing all week for Shabbos, the purpose of the week.

title.en: A heart like stone

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya on timtum halev, when the heart becomes like stone and one has no desire to daven, and brings the Gemara that forbidden food 'blocks' the heart, so that one no longer feels the joy of learning Torah.

title.en: Kashrus today and in the Tanya's time

summary.en: The Rav explains why a dulled heart is common today: packages of countless ingredients and lesser hechsherim, so one must be very careful about what one eats, as the Rambam explains on 'shomer piv'. In the Ba'al HaTanya's time food was cooked at home with yiras Shamayim and l'kavod Shabbos.

title.en: The taste and light of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Kuzmir chulent that tasted of Gan Eden because the Rebbe added beans 'l'kavod Shabbos kodesh', brings the Midrash on the special spice called Shabbos and on Shabbos being blessed with the light of a person's face, and describes how the Satmar Rav's face changed on Shabbos and each yom tov.

title.en: The Lechovitcher rebbetzin's candles

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Lechovitcher rebbetzin wept when her rich sister lit Shabbos candles, because she saw only a fire and not the light of Shabbos, adds that even electric light burns differently on Chol HaMoed, and brings Reb Mordechai of Lechovitch: one who does not work to feel the light of Shabbos will sit in Gan Eden like a log.

title.en: Wood that will not catch fire

summary.en: Back in the Tanya, the Rav explains that even in permitted things a person with a dull heart cannot hold back or sanctify himself, and brings the Zohar's advice of the head of the Heavenly yeshiva to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: wood that will not catch fire is chopped into small pieces, and so the body must be broken.

title.en: Why the soul's light does not take hold

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul wants to learn and daven with feeling, and one may understand Hashem's greatness with the mind, yet it does not reach the heart because of the body's coarseness, the strength of kelipas nogah. The remedy is to set times to humble oneself, for 'zivchei Elokim ruach nishbarah', a broken sitra achra.

title.en: Who is the 'I': beinoni and tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav asks who a person means when he says 'I'. For the beinoni it is his body and animal soul, and the neshamah is like a drink poured into him, as in 'Elokai neshamah shenasata bi'. For the tzaddik the soul is the person and the body his garment, as Hillel went to 'do kindness' with his body as with a stranger.

title.en: A worm and not a man; truth by levels

summary.en: The Rav explains Dovid's words 'I am a worm and not a man': a worm does what it was created for, while a man who does not is worse than a worm. He then asks whether a love felt in davening that fades afterwards was untrue, and answers that truth has levels: for the beinoni that is his truth.

title.en: Rebuking the body; the ger tzedek's candle

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's advice to speak to the body and rebuke its chutzpah in darkening the light of the soul. He tells of Graf Potocki, the ger tzedek, who answered his executioners that the smell of an extinguished Shabbos candle was sweeter to him than all their pleasures, and says this is what one tells the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: דברים שעושים טימטום הלב ואיך לתקן ולהזהר. בחינת האמת לפי מדריגתו. לפעמים אין התעוררות בשבת כי אז צריכים להיות במדריגה יותר זך. עצות כשיש טימטום הלב. למואס בגשמיות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 29, the Rav explains why a person suddenly cannot daven, why a higher level or a holier time demands a deeper teshuvah, and how to break the sitra achra through cheshbon hanefesh and seeing its nothingness before Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 29 on timtum halev, the closed heart that cannot daven. A hisorerus that fades after davening is still truth at a beinoni's level if it returns the next time. Sins of youth can block a person now, because above there is no time, and because each higher level needs a deeper teshuvah: Shabbos, Eretz Yisroel and every yahrzeit of a neshamah demand more than the weekday did. So a person who cannot daven should make a cheshbon hanefesh, like Dovid whose sin stood before him always. Even one without such sins can examine his wandering thoughts and his foolish dreams, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's Danzig story shows, yet without fear. He should then break himself with merirus, not atzvus, rebuke the sitra achra in his thoughts, and see that it is nullified before Hashem like darkness before light.

en: A beinoni's hisorerus that fades after davening is still truth at his level, as long as it comes back the next time.
Above there is no time, so a sin of long ago stands as if it were now, and teshuvah done once may not suffice for the present.
A higher level, whether in time (Shabbos), place (Eretz Yisroel) or the soul itself, demands a greater teshuvah, so a person may feel blocked exactly there.
When he cannot daven, a person should make a cheshbon hanefesh, perhaps Heaven wants to raise him higher and he must first do more teshuvah.
Even one without sins of youth can examine his thoughts and dreams, which show his soul does not ascend.
The breaking must come through merirus, which brings good counsel, and not through atzvus, which only puts one to sleep.
The sitra achra has no life of its own; it is nullified before Hashem like darkness before a lit candle.

title.en: Timtum halev and truth by one's level

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Tanya's counsel for a heart that is closed and cannot daven: to chop at it like a log that will not catch fire, and to make a cheshbon hanefesh. Reading on in chapter 29 and referring to chapter 13, he explains that truth has many levels, so a beinoni's arousal that returns each time is truth at his level.

title.en: Sins of youth, time, and the holiness of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that above there is no time, so a sin of youth stands as if committed now. With the parable of dressing for the street, a wedding and a king, he answers why one can daven on weekdays but not on Shabbos: Shabbos is the king's court and demands a greater teshuvah, and so too a holy place like Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The yahrzeit: a new judgment each year

summary.en: The Rav explains why on a yahrzeit people learn mishnayos and give tzedakah: each year the neshamah rises, and the cleansing that sufficed for last year's level is not enough for the next. In the same way a person in this world who is to rise higher needs a deeper teshuvah.

title.en: Cheshbon hanefesh and Dovid's sin before him

summary.en: The Rav says one who cannot daven should ask why, and consider that Heaven may want to raise him. He brings Dovid's words that his sin is before him always: at every higher step one sees the sin anew and must do teshuvah again. Even one who did not sin can make a cheshbon, as some do daily, for thoughts fly through the mind by the thousand.

title.en: Thoughts, dreams, and davening without fear

summary.en: The Rav explains that thoughts not for the sake of Heaven belong to the other side, and tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a man whose mind was in Danzig during davening. He then reads that foolish dreams show the soul does not ascend, and adds that this cheshbon must be made without fear, citing the tzaddikim's saying to think good and it will be good.

title.en: Breaking oneself: merirus, not atzvus

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's counsel to sit and think that one is nothing, not an honest servant of Hashem, and so break himself. He stresses the difference between merirus, which brings good counsel, and atzvus, which only puts one to sleep; through this the swollen sitra achra that blocks his davening is broken.

title.en: Rebuking the sitra achra in thought

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's call to thunder at the yetzer hara: not aloud but in thought, asking how long it will hide the light of Hashem, who fills all worlds and is unchanged by creation. Seeing the truth, that all existence is nothing before Hashem, he illustrates with a story of the Ba'al haTanya at his passing.

title.en: Like darkness before light; despising physicality

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sitra achra is nullified like darkness when a candle is lit, since its life is only sparks of kedushah it holds. He adds that darkness is itself a creation, and there is a holy darkness of tzimtzum, which is why the Tanya specifies physical light. He closes with the Tanya's counsel to despise physicality, which the yetzer uses to keep a person from davening.

catalogTitle: ט”ו בשבט: Tu Bishvat, Moshiach and Birthdays

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the Mishnah on Tu Bishvat gives Beis Shammai's view first, learns from it that a Jew who truly expects Moshiach acts on it, and teaches that a person's real birthday is the day he fulfills his mission.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah of the four Rosh Hashanahs and notes its unusual wording: instead of listing Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel side by side, it states the first of Shevat as the Rosh Hashanah for trees, as if ruling like Beis Shammai, and only then gives the fifteenth. The date decides which year fruit belongs to for terumah and maaser. Since there is a tradition that when Moshiach comes the halacha will follow Beis Shammai, a pious Jew goes out twice, on Rosh Chodesh Shevat and on Tu Bishvat; both views are real to him. From this the Rav learns what it means to be conscious of Moshiach, crediting the Lubavitcher Rebbe with making the world expect him. Turning to birthdays, he reads Pharaoh's birthday in Bereishis as the day he was born for his mission, and says each day carries such a mission.

en: The Rav explains that Rosh Hashanah for trees decides which year a tree's fruit belongs to for terumah and maaser, so the owner marks which trees have blossomed.
Because the halacha will follow Beis Shammai when Moshiach comes, the Rav says a pious Jew marks his trees both on Rosh Chodesh Shevat and on Tu Bishvat.
The Rav credits the Lubavitcher Rebbe with making the Jewish world conscious of Moshiach and expecting him every moment.
According to the Rav, a person's real birthday is the day he accomplishes the mission for which he was sent into the world.
The Rav says every day and every moment carries a mission, so each day can be a birthday.
