a person's mission in the world

title.en: The Mishnah's unusual wording on Tu Bishvat

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah of the four Rosh Hashanahs and asks why it states the first of Shevat as if ruling like Beis Shammai, instead of the usual form. He explains the halacha that terumah and maaser must be taken from fruit of the same year.

title.en: Marking the trees twice

summary.en: The Rav explains that the owner of a grove marks which trees have blossomed by Tu Bishvat, and that a pious Jew, mindful of the tradition that the halacha will follow Beis Shammai when Moshiach comes, marks them on Rosh Chodesh Shevat as well. This answers the Mishnah's wording: both opinions are relevant to us.

title.en: Living with Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav learns from the Mishnah that a Jew who truly believes in Moshiach expects him this year and acts on it. He addresses the Lubavitcher chassidim present and says the Lubavitcher Rebbe made the world conscious of Moshiach.

title.en: Pharaoh's birthday and the true birthday

summary.en: Turning to those celebrating a birthday, the Rav reads the Torah's phrase for Pharaoh's birthday as the day he was caused to be born, the day of his mission to free Yosef. He concludes that a person's real birthday is when he fulfills his mission, that every day carries a mission, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: הקדמה למזמור שיר ליום השבת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos it is Shabbos itself that sings to Hashem, and that our weekly Shabbos sings to the great Shabbos of the future, when all of history will be heard as one harmony.

abstract.en: The Rav opens a series on the meaning of the tefillos, saying that knowing what the words mean can bring warmth into davening, and begins with Shabbos and the chapter Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos. Every chapter of Tehillim has one theme running through it like a string through pearls; here the theme is that Shabbos itself sings. Creation was made in seven days like the seven notes of music, and only when the seventh day completes the seven-stringed harp can there be song; so too the seventh sea, the seventh land and King David are singers. From a Midrash that Adam said this chapter after learning the power of teshuvah, the Rav explains Shabbos and yovel as the return of everything to its root. Our Shabbos sings to the great Shabbos of the future, when the world will see that all of history, even the suffering of tzaddikim and of Klal Yisrael, was one harmony.

en: Every chapter of Tehillim has one theme threaded through all its verses, so the Rav first states a chapter's theme before translating its verses.
Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos does not mean a song about Shabbos but a song that Shabbos itself sings to Hashem.
Music needs all seven notes; the world, created in seven days, has its song only once Shabbos completes the seven-stringed harp.
Shabbos, like yovel, means the return of everything to its root, which is why the Midrash ties this chapter to teshuvah.
Our weekly Shabbos is a small Shabbos singing to the great Shabbos of the future, the day that is entirely Shabbos.
People cannot see how the suffering of tzaddikim and the success of the wicked fit together, but from Hashem's height it is all one harmony.

candidateTopics: teshuvah and return to the root

title.en: Why learn the meaning of the tefillos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah's mitzvah is to daven with the heart, and that in weak generations knowing the meaning of the words can bring warmth into davening. He begins with the Shabbos davening, notes that Lecha Dodi is a later custom, and that the Shulchan Aruch speaks of accepting Shabbos with Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos.

title.en: Tehillim as King David's portion in Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that every person has his own portion in the Torah, and the whole book of Tehillim is King David's portion, even chapters that Adam or Moshe said. He then explains that each chapter has one theme running through it like a string through pearls, so he will first give each chapter's content.

title.en: Shabbos sings: the seven notes of creation

summary.en: The Rav asks why the chapter is called a song of Shabbos when it says nothing about Shabbos, and answers that Shabbos itself sings. Through the seven 'kol' of Mizmor l'Dovid, the seven-stringed harp of the Beis Hamikdash and the seven notes of music, he explains that the world's harmony becomes song only when Shabbos completes the seven days.

title.en: The seventh is always the singer

summary.en: From a Midrash on the seventh day, the seventh sea and the seventh land, the Rav shows that the seventh always sings: the Kinneret, Eretz Yisrael, the zemer among the animals, and King David as the seventh of the ushpizin. He brings the Lechovitcher's saying about a Jew who can sing and does not sing on Shabbos, and the custom to sing Kel Adon with a tune.

title.en: Shabbos, teshuvah and yovel: return to the root

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Adam said this chapter when he heard from Kayin the power of teshuvah, and asks what Shabbos has to do with teshuvah. He explains that everything must return to its root, as in Koheles, the Maharal and the Ramban on yovel, and that Shabbos and above all the yovel bring back even the furthest Jew.

title.en: This year's yovel and the Shabbos of the future

summary.en: In passing, the Rav says that by the accepted reckoning this year, 5755, is a yovel year, discusses how the fiftieth year is counted, and mentions kavanos of the mekubalim for it. He then explains that in Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos the lower Shabbos sings to the higher one, the day that is entirely Shabbos, and expresses the hope that this year will be a time of favor for the redemption.

title.en: The questions of history and their tikkun

summary.en: The Rav describes the questions people ask on Hashem because of the suffering of Jews, from the Churban through the Crusades, the Inquisition and the six million, and says that we cannot answer but justify Hashem's judgment. He brings what the sefarim reveal: the martyrs of Tach v'Tat and the Asarah Harugei Malchus as rectifications of earlier sins, that Hashem never forgives a Jew's blood, and that before Moshiach souls are gathered into one generation for their tikkun.

title.en: Seeing the whole picture: the chapter's message

summary.en: The Rav reads the chapter's verses on Hashem's deep thoughts and His being on high, and gives the mashal of a fly on a Rembrandt painting that sees only a black spot. He tells his listeners to sing with Shabbos at the Shabbos table as a taste of the future Shabbos, and sums up the chapter with its last verse, explaining a word written without a vav as the hidden connection that is missing from our sight.

catalogTitle: מזמור שיר ליום השבת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos as the song the world of tikkun will sing over all of history, in which the good times and the dark times together make one harmony, like the ten-stringed asor and the sad-toned navel.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling Shabbos the return, the yovel, and links it to Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place, whose letters he finds in 'shir l'yom'. He explains why Shabbos is the day for 'tov lehodos': on Shabbos a Jew is equipped with extra powers to praise Hashem. On 'lehagid baboker chasdecha ve'emunascha baleilos' he brings Chavakuk, who based all the mitzvos on emunah, and a story of souls weary of gilgulim who were told to hold onto emunah. 'Alei asor' leads to the kinor of seven, eight and ten strings and the Sfas Emes on the new note of Moshiach's world. Through the piano's white and black keys he shows that joyful and sad times together form the melody of history. Rebbe Nachman, the Chazon Ish's tailor parable and stories of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk show that only the end reveals the meaning, and 'ki simachtani' closes it.

en: Shabbos is the Shabbos of time and Yerushalayim the Shabbos of place, so the words 'shir l'yom' share the letters of Yerushalayim.
Praising Hashem is an obligation every day, but on Shabbos a Jew is better equipped for it, with the neshamah yeseirah and freedom from physical concerns.
In the dark times before Moshiach the main demand of a Jew is emunah, knowing that everything is hashgacha pratis.
The kinor of the Mikdash had seven strings, Moshiach's will have eight and the final one ten, because the world to come will be too wonderful to be sung with seven notes.
Like the white and black keys of a piano, the good and bad times of history play together in one harmony, and the whole of history is Hashem's niggun.
Only at the end can one see why each painful event was needed, as the stories of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk show.

music and the days of Moshiach
good and bad times as one harmony

title.en: Shabbos and Yerushalayim: the place of return

summary.en: The Rav calls Shabbos the yovel and the return, explains the name Shabbos Hagadol, and shows that what exists in time exists in place: Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of geography, which is why 'shir l'yom' has its letters.

title.en: Why Shabbos is the day to praise

summary.en: On 'tov lehodos' the Rav brings the Radak and asks why Shabbos is singled out when one must praise Hashem always; he answers that on Shabbos a Jew is equipped with extra powers, and so Shabbos davening adds mizmorim and Nishmas.

title.en: Chavakuk, emunah and the weary souls

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on emunah, tells of souls weary of endless gilgulim who were told by Hashem to grab onto emunah, and explains 'emunascha baleilos' as holding onto emunah in the dark times of hester panim.

title.en: Alei asor: the strings of the kinor

summary.en: The Rav describes the song of Shabbos as a look back over the journey of exile, then brings Rav Hirsch and the Gemara on the kinor of seven, eight and ten strings, explains the octave, and speaks of the wisdom of music.

title.en: The eighth note and the ten maamaros

summary.en: Following the Sfas Emes, the Rav explains that Moshiach's world will need a new eighth note, illustrating with phone-number combinations, and ties the ten strings to the ten maamaros, when Jews will rise above the angels.

title.en: Asor and navel, white keys and black keys

summary.en: The Rav reads asor as richness and navel as withering, describes the piano's white and black keys, says that inventions spread over the world come with hashgacha, and explains white as chesed and black as din through doctors' and Kohanim's white clothing.

title.en: History as one symphony

summary.en: The Rav applies alei asor and alei navel to the history of every nation and every Jew: bad times are part of the harmony, so one blesses on the bad as on the good and says gam zu letovah, and 'higayon b'chinor' means to contemplate the whole world as Hashem's instrument.

title.en: Every life a niggun; the tailor's silk

summary.en: The Rav brings Rebbe Nachman that every person's life is a niggun, then the Chazon Ish's answer about the six million with the parable of a tailor cutting silk, and points to the rebuilding of Torah in Eretz Yisrael while the garment is still being sewn.

title.en: Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk and 'ki simachtani'

summary.en: The Rav tells of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk healing a melamed through anger, and of his refusal of Russian citizenship, which sent his followers to Siberia and saved them; he concludes that we are blind until the end, and with 'ki simachtani' that the wonders we do understand let us trust those we don't.

catalogTitle: Ocean Waves: The Striving of the Rising Waves

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that ocean waves are the lower waters straining to rise toward Hashem, and tells the bochurim that unlike the waves, a Jew who strives to rise in Torah will get there.

abstract.en: The Rav praises the bochurim who devote themselves to Torah and avodas Hashem despite today's temptations, saying the Shechinah has nachas from them. He shares a thought from that morning, when he watched the sunrise over the ocean and the high waves crashing on the sand. Why does the sea have waves? Physics is not the final answer, since Hashem made its laws for a reason. At creation the waters were separated into upper and lower waters, and the lower waters weep, wanting to be near the King. Nisuch hamayim gave them a way to serve Hashem; since the Churban they weep again, and the Yismach Moshe reads the weeping by the rivers of Babylon in this light. The waves are the waters trying to rise; they never succeed, yet Hashem praises their effort. A Jew is different: if he yearns and struggles, he will get there. The Rav closes with 'ashreichem'.

en: The Shechinah has nachas from bochurim who devote themselves to Torah and avodas Hashem despite the temptations of the time.
The laws of physics that make waves were themselves created by Hashem for a spiritual reason.
The lower waters, separated from the upper waters at creation, weep because they want to be near the King.
The waves are the lower waters trying to rise; they cannot succeed, yet Hashem praises them for trying.
Unlike the waves, a Jew who yearns and struggles to rise in Torah will get there.

title.en: Praise for the bochurim; sunrise over the ocean

summary.en: The Rav praises the bochurim who devote themselves to Torah despite today's temptations and says the Shechinah has nachas from them. Pressed for time, he shares a thought from that morning, when he watched the sunrise over the ocean and the high waves crashing on the sand.

title.en: Why the waves rise: the weeping lower waters

summary.en: The Rav asks why the sea has waves and answers from the separation of the waters at creation: the lower waters weep to be near the King. He brings nisuch hamayim, the Churban, the Yismach Moshe on the rivers of Babylon, and the passuk in Tehillim that Hashem praises the rising waves for trying, though they can never reach.

title.en: A Jew who strives will get there

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim they are not like the waves: a Jew who yearns and struggles to rise in Torah will reach his goal, as many who found learning hard when young did. He closes with 'ashreichem' and the assurance that they will bring nachas ruach to the Shechinah.

catalogTitle: כי שמחתני ה' בפעלך וכו'

oneLiner.en: Going through Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos, the Rav explains that on Shabbos a Jew sees the harmony of creation and rejoices even in what he cannot understand, knowing that the wicked flourish like grass only to wither while Klal Yisrael, rooted in unity and in the 'eighth' level above nature, endures forever.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the second half of Psalm 92. At the end of days every question will be answered; on Shabbos, freed from the week's toil, a person looks at the harmony of creation, sings, and concludes that what he does not understand also has deep answers. Following the Rambam, contemplating creation leads to love of Hashem. The 'ish ba'ar' knows he cannot understand Hashem's ways; the fool turns this into a question about why the wicked prosper. The wicked are like grass that sprouts first and withers first, as a story of a Jew forced off a plane that later crashed illustrates. Hashem is 'marom', beyond reach; empires vanished while Jews remained. The Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that seeing Hashem behind every enemy sweetens the judgments. Evil belongs to division, Shabbos to unity; the world decays since Adam's sin, but Klal Yisrael, like the Chanukah oil, belongs to the eternal 'eighth', and the tzaddik grows slowly like a palm and lasts forever.

en: On Shabbos, free from the week's labor, a person contemplates the harmony of creation and sings, and from what he sees he concludes that what he does not understand also has deep answers.
The 'ish ba'ar' at least knows that Hashem's ways are beyond him, while the fool takes his own lack of understanding as a question against Hashem.
The wicked are like grass, the first to sprout in spring and the first to wither, so their success is only for their eventual destruction.
The great empires that oppressed the Jews, Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, came to nothing, while the Jews remained.
Everything holy is unity and everything opposed to holiness is division; Shabbos is the secret of oneness, so the wicked, who belong to division, cannot endure it.
Since Adam's sin everything in the seven days of creation must end, but the Jewish soul belongs to the 'eighth', above nature, and will live to see the eternal Shabbos.
The tzaddik is not like grass but like a palm and a cedar: he grows slowly and lasts forever.

title.en: Ki simachtani: singing on Shabbos about creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that at the end of days all questions will be answered, and that on Shabbos, freed from the week's toil, a person looks at the beauty and harmony of creation and sings. From what he sees he understands that Hashem's thoughts are very deep, and that what he does not understand also has brilliant answers.

title.en: Ish ba'ar, the fool, and the wicked like grass

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that contemplating creation leads to love of Hashem, then explains that the 'ish ba'ar' knows he cannot understand Hashem's conduct while the fool asks the old question why the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. He answers with the parable of grass, which sprouts first in spring and withers first at summer's end.

title.en: The seat on the plane from Morocco

summary.en: The Rav says that the success of a rasha can be his downfall and the troubles of a tzaddik his success, and tells of a Jewish businessman who was forced to give up his seat on a plane from Morocco to an Arab sheikh; the plane crashed, and the man made a seudas hodaah.

title.en: Hashem is marom; empires come and go

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes 'gavoha', high but rising from the ground, from 'marom', high and detached like a cloud, and says Hashem's ways are marom, beyond reach. On 'ki hinei oyvecha' he shows how Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome vanished like waves breaking on the shore, while the Jews remained.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov: Hashem behind every enemy

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that every trouble a Jew suffers from people is Hashem in disguise; when a Jew recognizes this the judgments are sweetened and the kelipah breaks, and this is how he reads 'ki hinei oyvecha'. He then explains that holiness is unity and its opposite is division, bringing Chazal's contrast between Yaakov's 'nefesh' and Esav's 'nafshos'.

title.en: Yom echad, the second day, and Shabbos as oneness

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on why the first day is called 'yom echad', and explains that on the second day division, Gehinnom and evil were created, connecting this to the Gemara on pairs. Shabbos is 'raza d'echad', so the wicked, who belong to division, cannot exist on it and are scattered, while Klal Yisrael's horn is raised.

title.en: Everything decays since Adam; the eighth above nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that through Adam's sin decay came upon all of creation, so everything in the seven days of creation must end, but not the Jewish people, who will live to see the eternal Shabbos. He brings the Maharal's concept of the 'eighth world' above the limits of the seven of nature, and the Gemara that the harp of the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and that of Moshiach will have eight.

title.en: Wine and oil, Torah and the Chanukah oil

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah was given on the fiftieth day, entering the eighth week, because it comes from heaven. Wine, whose value is seventy, belongs to the seven, while oil, from the word 'shemonah', rises above every liquid and does not spoil; the Chanukah oil, which was not consumed, lasted eight days. That oil, revealed to Yaakov, is 'shemen ra'anan', the endless existence of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Tishmanah oznai and the tzaddik like a palm

summary.en: The Rav explains that the nations look at the Jew and plan his end, but Klal Yisrael has a hidden ruach hakodesh that hears 'from behind the curtain' that it will outlive them, as Jews sang in the camps. He closes with the tzaddik who is not like quick grass but like a palm and a cedar, growing slowly and lasting forever.

catalogTitle: צדיק כתמר וכו'

oneLiner.en: Learning the end of Mizmor Shir leYom HaShabbos and the start of Hashem Malach, the Rav explains that the tzaddik flourishes like the date palm and the cedar, and that when Moshiach comes everyone will see that all of Hashem's hidden din was really rachamim.

abstract.en: The Rav contrasts the wicked, who sprout like grass and wither at the end of the season, with the tzaddik who flourishes like the date palm. A fruit tree does not grow tall because its strength goes into its fruit, while the cedar grows tall but gives no fruit; the tzaddik who gives his strength to his students is promised siyata dishmaya and has both, as shown from the chassidim rishonim and the Chasam Sofer's children. He stresses being planted in the right place, bringing the Rambam and the Kuzari, and explains that Klal Yisrael will blossom only when the galus ends. 'Lehagid ki yashar Hashem' means that in the future all suffering will be seen as good; he illustrates midas hadin through the combinations of the Name in Nissan, Teves and Tammuz. On Hashem Malach he explains that Hashem's apparent aloofness is only a garment, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's worm story, and that in the mixed-up world of 'tevel' Hashem still holds everything firm.

en: The wicked are like grass that flourishes quickly and withers at the reckoning, while the tzaddik is like the date palm that grows slowly but endures forever.
A tzaddik who gives his strength to his students does not lose by it: Hashem gives him siyata dishmaya, so he is both fruitful like the palm and tall like the cedar.
A person must be planted in the right place, among tzaddikim and ehrliche Yidden, to grow; Klal Yisrael too could not blossom in galus.
'Lehagid ki yashar Hashem' teaches that in the days of Moshiach it will be revealed that all the din Jews suffered was rachamim inside and for their good.
Hashem's apparent aloofness, 'gei'us lavesh', is only a garment; underneath He watches over every smallest creature with hashgachah pratis.
The world is called 'tevel', a mixture in which one cannot see clearly, yet Hashem holds it firm and sometimes sends a flash of open miracles.

combinations of the Name Havayah in the months

title.en: The palm and the grass

summary.en: The Rav opens the passuk 'tzaddik katamar yifrach' against the earlier verses about the wicked who sprout like grass. He explains that a fruit tree stays low because its strength goes into its fruit while the cedar grows tall without fruit, and compares this to teachers who give their strength to their students.

title.en: Giving to others costs nothing

summary.en: The Rav says the tzaddik is promised siyata dishmaya so he does not lose by teaching others, bringing the chassidim rishonim who davened nine hours a day and the Chasam Sofer, whose student answered his worry about his children with 'kol hayom chonen umalveh'. The tzaddik has both the palm's fruit and the cedar's height.

title.en: Planted in the house of Hashem

summary.en: After Rav Hirsch's reading, the Rav explains 'shesulim b'veis Hashem': the tzaddik is planted in the beis medrash, like the golden trees of the Beis Hamikdash. He stresses being in the right place, with the Rambam and the Kuzari's tree that needs its own soil, and explains that Klal Yisrael will blossom anew at the end of galus, 'od yenuvun beseivah'.

title.en: Lehagid ki yashar Hashem

summary.en: The Rav calls 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem' the summary of the chapter: it looks unfair that tzaddikim suffer and the wicked succeed, but later it will be revealed that everything was for Klal Yisrael's good. He brings Reb Nachum that even the nations will then grasp that Jews in galus were happier than they, with 'az yimalei schok pinu'.

title.en: Din and rachamim in the months

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that in the future only 'hatov vehameitiv' will be said, since din will be seen as a garment over rachamim. He explains that each month has its own combination of the Name Havayah: Nissan, from 'yismechu hashamayim', is pure chessed, while Teves is a month of din connected to Esav, softened by the Chanukah lights.

title.en: Tammuz: the Name written backwards

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tammuz, whose combination comes from 'vechol zeh einenu shoveh li' fully backwards, holds the harshest din, worse than Av. Yet when Moshiach comes it will be seen that Havayah was always straight, and the troubles of all the generations will be understood as 'ki yashar Hashem'.

title.en: Hashem Malach: the garment of pride

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem Malach continues the previous chapter, which is why they are said together at Kabbalas Shabbos, and that looking back from Moshiach one will say Hashem 'malach', He always reigned. With a mashal of a proud man who ignores small people, he explains that Hashem only seems aloof, as the apikorsim claim, but 'hamashpili lir'os' He watches over everything.

title.en: The worm and the hidden face

summary.en: The Rav tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a breeze Hashem sent for a suffering worm, and explains that 'gei'us lavesh' is a garment over a garment, hester within hester. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's mashal of a child in the forest who does not see his father watching, and a deeper hiding where he does not even know.

title.en: Af tikon tevel: the world holds firm

summary.en: The Rav explains 'af tikon tevel bal timot': people fear the world will be destroyed, as the Dor Haflagah built a tower to hold up the sky, but Hashem watches over it. He explains that 'tevel' means a mixture, a world where one does not see clearly, yet at times like Chanukah and Purim Hashem sends a flash of light, 'he'iru verakav tevel'.

catalogTitle: Kashrus: An address to Organizations of Kashrus Overseers

oneLiner.en: The Rav tells kashrus supervisors that, just as evil entered the world through food and Pharaoh made his food officials ministers of tumah, they are Heaven's appointed ministers of kedushah, who must work together without rivalry.

abstract.en: After a short introduction by the host, the Rav recalls that Adam was meant to remain in Gan Eden, but was driven out for a sin of eating. Forbidden food, he explains, defiles the body and stops up the heart, becomes part of a person's very flesh and blood, and leaves no desire for Torah and tefillah; the Rema warns about this even for an infant. He then notes that Pharaoh, unlike a modern head of state, made the officials in charge of drink, bread and meat into ministers, because he knew that tumah is best spread through food. Yosef HaTzaddik was his counterpart in kedushah. Turning to the kashrus supervisors, the Rav calls them the ministers of kedushah, cites the example of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz who supported other yeshivos, and warns against competition. He closes with the angels who visited Avraham Avinu, strengthened by his holy food for their mission to save Lot and the line of Moshiach.

en: Adam was driven from Gan Eden not for idolatry, immorality or bloodshed but for eating what he was forbidden to eat.
Forbidden food defiles the body, stops up the heart and becomes part of a person's flesh and blood, taking away his desire for Torah and tefillah.
Pharaoh made the officials over food into ministers of state because he knew that tumah spreads best through food.
The kashrus supervisors are Heaven's appointed ministers of kedushah and taharah, the counterpart of Pharaoh's ministers of food.
Ministers of one government must cooperate rather than compete, for they all serve the same Master.
A supervisor who is especially careful puts kedushah into all the food his company produces.

title.en: Adam's sin was a sin of eating

summary.en: After the host's introduction, the Rav explains that Adam lost Gan Eden through eating forbidden food, and describes how forbidden food defiles the body, stops up the heart and removes the desire for Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Pharaoh's ministers of food

summary.en: The Rav asks why Pharaoh had ministers over drink, bread and meat when a modern president only has a chef, and explains that Pharaoh, the master of tumah, knew that tumah is spread through food; Yosef HaTzaddik was his counterpart in kedushah.

title.en: Ministers of kedushah must not compete

summary.en: The Rav tells the kashrus supervisors that they are the ministers of kedushah, brings the example of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz who sent his best talmidim to found other yeshivos, and warns that ministers who compete ruin their country; one cannot touch what is destined for another.

title.en: The angels strengthened by Avraham's food

summary.en: From the week's sedra the Rav explains that angels too receive nourishment, and that the angels who ate at Avraham Avinu were fortified by the kedushah of his food for their dangerous mission to save Lot, from whom Moshiach descends. He closes by urging the supervisors to cooperate and sanctify the Jewish kitchen.

catalogTitle: ה' מלך גאות לבש

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 93, the Rav explains that Hashem's kingship is hidden throughout the galus, and that when Moshiach comes it will be revealed that He was always King and everything was for the good of the Jewish people.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Tehillim 93, which continues Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos and speaks of the time of Moshiach, when it will be revealed retroactively that Hashem was always King. Following the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, he explains that the akeidah's real test was not the slaughter itself but Avraham's unanswered question against Hashem's promise; this is the last test of our generation too. He reads the psalm verse by verse: the rivers and the breakers of the sea are the kingdoms that rose against Israel, and Hashem on high is mightier. A second reading, from a Midrash on the lower waters and the Yismach Moshe on Al naharos Bavel, has the rivers weeping with Israel and hoping. Eidosecha are the prophets or Klal Yisrael itself, faithful to Hashem's house. He ends with Chad Gadya and with Tehillim 29, where all beauty and strength are ascribed to Hashem, unlike Greek and American culture.

en: Hashem malach refers to the time of Moshiach, when it will be revealed that Hashem was always King, even through the hiding of the galus.
The test of the akeidah was that Avraham had a question against Hashem's promise and was not given the answer; this is also the last test of the present generation.
The rivers and the breakers of the sea in the psalm are the kingdoms and empires that tried to drown Israel, and Hashem on high is mightier than all of them.
In a second reading, the rivers weep over the Beis Hamikdash together with Israel, and the Jewish people's hope to return is itself their strength.
Klal Yisrael are Hashem's witnesses: their very existence, after all the kingdoms have vanished, testifies that Hashem exists and gave the Torah.
Tehillim 29 teaches that all beauty and strength must be ascribed to Hashem, against the Greek culture of deifying strength and beauty that rules America today.

korbanos and the elevation of creation

title.en: Hashem malach and the test of the akeidah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tehillim 93 continues the Shabbos psalm and speaks of the time of Moshiach, when Hashem's hidden kingship will be revealed. With the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, he turns to the akeidah as the last and hardest test and asks why it was a test at all.

title.en: A question without an answer

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham's real test was that his madreigos were taken from him and he had a question against Hashem's promise, and he was not given the answer that every child learning Chumash with Rashi knows. This is the test of our generation, full of questions; when Moshiach comes all will be answered, and it will be seen that Hashem was always King.

title.en: The rivers and the breakers are the kingdoms

summary.en: The Rav explains nachon kis'acha me'az: Hashem was always King, but the world, olam, is from he'elem, hiddenness. Following the commentators, the rising rivers are the kingdoms that oppressed Israel in galus and the breakers of the sea are the great empires, yet Hashem on high is mightier and they will come to their downfall.

title.en: The weeping of the lower waters

summary.en: The Rav offers another reading from a Midrash: the lower waters cried that they were not close to the King, and Hashem promised them nisuch hamayim and the salt on the mizbe'ach, through which all of creation is brought close through korbanos. After the churban the waters wept again, and he brings the Yismach Moshe on gam bachinu: the rivers of Bavel wept, and Israel wept too.

title.en: The rivers' cry and Israel's hope

summary.en: On this reading, the rivers raise their voice in weeping over the Beis Hamikdash and Israel identifies with them. Mishberei yam is read as hope, like Rashi's reading of shever in Mitzrayim, and the hope that Hashem on high will rebuild His house is itself Israel's strength and comfort in galus.

title.en: Eidosecha ne'emnu me'od

summary.en: With Rashi, the Rav explains that Hashem's witnesses are the prophets, whose promises of redemption we trust, and that the whole galus is a journey to Hashem's house, like the masa'os in the wilderness. He then reads the witnesses as Klal Yisrael itself, whose existence testifies to Hashem, and explains ne'emnu as firm and loyal, and the form eidosecha as pointing to the weak sheep among seventy wolves.

title.en: L'orech yamim and Chad Gadya

summary.en: The Rav explains that l'orech yamim refers to the day that is entirely Shabbos and to the third Beis Hamikdash, which will never again be destroyed, when Hashem remains alone with His people. He brings the Chasam Sofer's reading of Chad Gadya: kingdom after kingdom swallows the little goat, and in the end Hashem remains with His Chad Gadya.

title.en: Havu laShem: ascribing all strength to Hashem

summary.en: Turning to Tehillim 29 sung at Kabbalas Shabbos, the Rav recalls its seven kolos, matching the seven days of creation and the seven strings of the harp, and explains that Shabbos is malchus, when everything good and strong is ascribed to Hashem. He contrasts this with Greek culture that deifies strength and beauty, explains that Edom includes all the earlier kingdoms, and brings Reb Feivel Mendlowitz's remark that the leviathan's stomach is in America.

catalogTitle: מזמור לדוד הבו לה' בני אלים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Mizmor l'David, Havu laShem bnei elim, as the chapter of bitul, giving all strength and beauty back to Hashem, and shows why this is how one receives Shabbos, the day of Hashem's kingship.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the place of Mizmor l'David at the end of Kabbalas Shabbos and the Gemara that ties its eighteen Names and seven 'voices' to the eighteen weekday brachos and the seven of Shabbos. Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, he reads the chapter as a call to the mighty to credit all strength and beauty to Hashem and to hear 'the voice of Hashem' inside them. Since bitul is the attribute of malchus, which belongs to Shabbos and to David HaMelech, this is the chapter for receiving Shabbos. He explains that bitul is the purpose of creation, to be completed when the whole world recognizes Hashem, and illustrates it with stories of tzaddikim. True humility, he says, is joy and nullification, not depression, shown by Yishmael's teshuvah and by Yosef joining his brothers' minyan. He ends with the Gemara and Rashi on the verses and with Hashem's voice in destruction and rebuilding.

en: The Gemara links the eighteen Names in this chapter to the eighteen weekday brachos and its seven 'voices' to the seven brachos of Shabbos, so the chapter stands on the border between weekday and Shabbos.

Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the chapter tells the mighty and the beautiful that their strength and beauty are Hashem's, and that one should hear 'the voice of Hashem' speaking out of every strength and beauty in the world.
Bitul to Hashem is the attribute of malchus, which is revealed on Shabbos and embodied by David HaMelech, and this is why the chapter is used to receive Shabbos.
Bitul is the purpose of a person's service and of all creation, as Shabbos is the purpose of creation, and it will be completed when the whole world recognizes Hashem's kingship.
True humility is not going about broken and depressed but being happy that one has so great a Creator and nullifying oneself to His will.
Hachna'ah, yielding to Hashem, to tzaddikim, to friends and to every creature, includes everything, and its truest form is reached on Shabbos.
The same 'voice of Hashem' heard in the world's beauty is in its destruction too, and Hashem can rebuild what was destroyed and make even the wilderness bloom.

candidateTopics: Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch on Tehillim

title.en: Mizmor l'David between weekday and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav places Mizmor l'David after Lecha Dodi in Kabbalas Shabbos and brings the Gemara linking its eighteen Names to the eighteen weekday brachos and its seven 'voices' to the seven brachos of Shabbos. He notes that receiving the extra soul of Shabbos fully requires immersing in a mikvah erev Shabbos.

title.en: Rav Hirsch: give all strength to Hashem

summary.en: Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the Rav reads the chapter as a call to the strong and the beautiful to credit their might and honor to Hashem and bow before Him. He explains 'the voice of Hashem is in strength, in beauty': in every power and every beautiful thing one should hear Hashem speaking.

title.en: Why this chapter receives Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that bitul is the attribute of malchus, revealed on Shabbos and embodied by David HaMelech, the seventh of the ushpizin. He brings the Gemara that Avraham, Moshe and David each made themselves nothing, and the Chasam Sofer's point that father, teacher and king all did so, and concludes that Shabbos is the day to proclaim oneself Hashem's creation.

title.en: Bitul, the purpose of creation

summary.en: The Rav brings the usual commentators' reading of Havu laShem, then explains that bitul is the purpose of man and of creation, to be completed in the days of Moshiach when all the world recognizes Hashem, as one prays on Rosh Hashanah. He tells how Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz twirled a window-shade string during Shemoneh Esrei, praying that even the string should know it was created by Hashem.

title.en: What true humility is

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Maggid of Mezritch sending for the Baal HaTanya, who was singing 'veyeda kol pa'ul' at his shtender. He then explains that humility is not depression but joyful bitul, that a tzaddik may praise himself while being nothing in his own eyes, and tells of the youngest son of Rav Mordechai of Chernobyl, who took 'nothing' as his share.

title.en: Yishmael and Yosef: the sign of hachna'ah

summary.en: The Rav shows that Yishmael's teshuvah was seen in his yielding to Yitzchak, and brings the Igra deKallah's answer to why Yosef never wrote to his father: the brothers had bound the Shechinah by an oath, and Yosef himself joined to make their minyan. He concludes that the heart of Yiddishkeit is bitul to Hashem, to tzaddikim, to friends and to every creature.

title.en: Shabbos, Yerushalayim and seeing Hashem in everything

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos, when a Jew produces nothing, is the day to reach bitul, and brings the Baal HaTanya that true prostration needs the holiness of Yerushalayim. He ties Rav Hirsch's reading to the Baal Shem Tov's teaching of seeing Hashem in food, beauty and every object, and tells how Rav Eizikel of Komarna saw only holy Names before his eyes.

title.en: The three havu and the first three brachos

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that bnei elim are the children of the Avos and the Gemara that derives the first three brachos of Shemoneh Esrei from the three 'havu'. He brings the Radak that the waters are the nations, and the Gemara that 'Kel hakavod hir'im' is the source of the nineteenth bracha against the wicked.

title.en: The voice of Hashem in destruction and rebuilding

summary.en: The Rav explains the breaking of the cedars of Lebanon as Hashem humbling the mighty nations, and with Rav Hirsch teaches that the same voice of Hashem heard in beauty is in destruction and in the shifting of nations' borders. He ends with 'kol Hashem yachil midbar': Hashem can make even the wilderness bloom, as Midbar Kadesh became a great house of learning.

catalogTitle: קול ה' יחולל אילות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains 'kol Hashem yecholel ayalos' as the last, hardest blow of exile that brings the birth of the geulah, and 'Hashem lamabul yashav' as the flood that turned into the gift of Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the seventh 'kol' of Mizmor 29 as the coming of the great Shabbos, when the 'forests' that hide Hashem's kingship are stripped bare and only His glory is heard. He brings the Midrash on the ayalah that cannot give birth until a snake strikes her: so too Klal Yisrael, before the geulah things get worse, as in Egypt when Pharaoh's decree took away the Shabbos rest. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that the beaten shotrim had sacrificed themselves for Shabbos. He brings Rabbi Moshe of Sambor's reading of 'ki ayal ta'arog': the tzaddik forgets his own pain and davens for kavod Shamayim. On 'Hashem lamabul yashav' he says the darkness before Moshiach is like the flood and one must not despair. Through Rashi's Midrash on Matan Torah he explains that rain carries spiritual blessing, and the flood was Torah that came down as gashmiyus. He ends that in the season of tal umatar one davens for the rain of Torah.

en: The seventh 'kol' of Mizmor 29 corresponds to the coming great Shabbos, when the 'forests' that hide Hashem's kingship are stripped away and only His glory is heard in the rebuilt Beis Hamikdash.
Like the ayalah that can only give birth after the snake's blow, Klal Yisrael lacks the strength to bring the geulah, and just before it the exile becomes harder.
Pharaoh's decree was aimed at the Shabbos rest the Jews had won in Egypt, and the shotrim who were beaten for the shortfall were giving their lives for Shabbos.
A tzaddik in his own suffering does not pray for himself but for the honor of Hashem's Name, like the ayalah that forgets her own pains and prays for water for the world.
The present darkness before Moshiach resembles the time of the flood, when Hashem 'sat alone', and just as then He was afterward acknowledged as King forever, so one must not despair now.

Every physical flow from Heaven, such as rain, carries a spiritual flow within it; the flood was Torah that came down in physical form because the generation was unworthy, and at Matan Torah the same flow came down as Torah.

candidateTopics: Pharaoh's decree and Shabbos in Egypt
tal umatar as prayer for Torah

title.en: The seventh kol: the great Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the seven 'kolos' of Mizmor 29 parallel the seven days, and reads the seventh, 'kol Hashem yecholel ayalos vayechesof ye'aros', as the coming of the great Shabbos. Then the 'forests', the nations who hide Hashem's kingship like trees hiding the sky, are stripped away, and in the rebuilt Beis Hamikdash only His glory is heard.

title.en: The ayalah, the snake and the birth of the geulah

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Iyov and the Midrash that the ayalah cannot give birth until Hashem sends a snake to strike her. The Midrash's hint is Klal Yisrael, who lack the strength to bring the geulah, so before it comes a blow and the exile grows harder, as in the parsha when Moshe was sent and the bondage became worse.

title.en: Pharaoh's decree against Shabbos and the last blow

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash that the Jews worked at full capacity from the first day, and asks with the Chasam Sofer how the straw decree could add anything. He answers that Moshe had won them a Shabbos rest, which Pharaoh's decree aimed to take away, so the shotrim who were beaten had sacrificed themselves for Shabbos. He then applies the snake's blow to the present, the Holocaust and the worsening exile, as the last tremor before the birth of Moshiach.

title.en: 'Ki ayal ta'arog': praying for kavod Shamayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk 'ki ayal ta'arog al afikei mayim' and the question of Rabbi Moshe of Sambor why it mixes a masculine noun with a feminine verb. He answers that the ayalah in her own birth pains forgets herself and prays for water for the world as if she were a male, and so the tzaddikim in exile pray not for their own troubles but for the honor of Hashem's Name.

title.en: 'Hashem lamabul yashav': do not despair

summary.en: The Rav describes the darkest hour before Moshiach, when the world is more lawless than the generation of the flood and it seems Hashem has left it. He reads 'Hashem lamabul yashav' to say that history repeats: at the flood too Hashem sat alone, and afterward 'vayeshev Hashem melech l'olam', so one must not despair.

title.en: Rashi's Midrash and the spirituality within rain

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash cited by Rashi that at Matan Torah the nations, hearing the great sounds, asked Bilam whether Hashem was bringing a flood. To explain it he sets out a principle: every physical flow from Heaven, like rain, carries a spiritual flow, as the Gemara in Taanis says, and the same flow takes different forms, like ice, water and steam.

title.en: Noach, Moshe and the flood as Torah

summary.en: The Rav says the time of the flood was an eis ratzon to give the Torah, and brings the Gemara in Chullin and the Zohar that Noach's soul was Moshe's; because Noach did not pray for his generation the waters are called 'mei Noach', which Moshe repaired with 'mecheini na'. He explains that 'geshem' comes from gashmiyus, that a tzaddik davening for rain means Torah, and that the flood was Torah that came down in physical form and turned to destruction.

title.en: The flood of Torah and davening for tal umatar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that a Jew in Krias Shema asks for grain, wine and oil of Torah, and explains that the nations' wise men saw in the stars the same arrangement as at the flood; Bilam answered that this time the flood comes as Torah, 'Hashem oz l'amo yiten', a threefold Torah of the shin in 'bashalom'. He closes that in the season of tal umatar a ben Torah should know he is davening for the rain of Torah, and the winter is the time for deep learning.

catalogTitle: Emunah - The Everlasting Essence of a Jewish Heart

oneLiner.en: The Rav opens a series on the mitzvah of emunah, explaining that it is the foundation of all the mitzvos and a hereditary trait inherited from Avraham Avinu, a spark that cannot be extinguished in any Jewish heart.

abstract.en: The Rav describes how, decades ago, he began teaching the mitzvos from the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges them by the limbs of the body and opens the mitzvos of the heart with emunah; over time his notes grew until he taught only emunah for a whole year. Emunah, he says, must be spoken about and fed constantly, like daily food, citing Yirmiyahu and Tehillim, and former students later thanked him for preparing them for challenges. Emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and is renewed through Shema. He presents the dispute of the Rambam, who counts emunah among the 613 mitzvos, and the Ramban, who sees it as their prerequisite, since it is not phrased as a command. To approach the Rambam he distinguishes acquired from hereditary knowledge, using the bee, beaver and spider, and says emunah is a Jew's hereditary instinct from Sinai and Avraham Avinu. A kashya on this, like a helium balloon to a child, does not disprove it.

en: Emunah is the first mitzvah of the heart in the Sefer Chareidim and the first of the Ten Commandments, which shows it is the most important mitzvah.
Emunah must be constantly fortified and fed, just as a person cannot eat one breakfast for his whole life.
The Rambam counts emunah among the 613 mitzvos, while the Ramban holds it is above them, their foundation and prerequisite, since without emunah no act is a mitzvah.
Some knowledge is hereditary rather than acquired, as with the bee, the beaver and the spider, and emunah in a Jew is such a hereditary instinct.
Every Jew's soul remembers hearing 'Anochi Hashem' at Sinai, and Jews inherited emunah from Avraham Avinu, so a spark of emunah remains in every Jewish heart.

Rambam and Ramban on counting emunah
Avraham Avinu as the first believer
spark of emunah in every Jew

title.en: The Sefer Chareidim's order of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav recalls beginning to teach the mitzvos from the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges them by the limbs of the body rather than by the order of the Torah. He explains that the heart governs the emotional mitzvos such as tefillah, dveikus and love of Hashem, and that the first mitzvah of the heart is emunah.

title.en: Emunah must be fed constantly

summary.en: The Rav tells how his shiurim narrowed until he taught only the mitzvah of emunah for a whole year. Citing Yirmiyahu's rebuke and the passuk in Tehillim, he says emunah must be spoken about and nourished daily, and recounts how former students thanked him years later for preparing them for challenges to their emunah.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban: is emunah one of the 613?

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and is renewed through Shema several times a day. He presents the dispute of the Rambam, who counts emunah as a mitzvah, and the Ramban, who calls it the prerequisite of all the mitzvos, illustrated by tzedakah given without emunah. He adds that every mitzvah is phrased as a command while 'Anochi' is a statement, which seems to support the Ramban, and says the Rambam's view must be understood.

title.en: Hereditary knowledge: the bee, the beaver, the spider

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes hereditary traits such as hair color from acquired knowledge such as a sugya in Bava Metzia, then shows that some knowledge is inherited: a bee builds a honeycomb, a beaver a dam and a spider a web without being taught. He concludes that emunah in a Jew is such a hereditary instinct.

title.en: A spark of emunah from Sinai and Avraham Avinu

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew's soul remembers hearing 'Anochi Hashem' at Sinai, and that Avraham Avinu, the first believer, completed creation, so Jews are believers the sons of believers. He raises the kashya of Jews who do not believe and, with the mashal of a child seeing a helium balloon rise, explains that a kashya does not disprove an absolute truth. He closes that a spark of emunah in every Jewish heart cannot be extinguished, deferring the answers to the next shiur.

catalogTitle: הקדמה לפסד"ז

oneLiner.en: Opening his study of Pesukei d'Zimra, the Rav explains that davening is a climb through the worlds to stand before the King, that every word of tefillah is a palace, and that Pesukei d'Zimra cut a path through the angel-filled atmosphere together with Dovid Hamelech.

abstract.en: Having finished the chapters connected to Kabbalas Shabbos, the Rav begins Pesukei d'Zimra. The goal of davening is Shemoneh Esrei, standing before the King, and the way there passes through the four worlds: korbanos, Pesukei d'Zimra, the blessings of Shema, then Shemoneh Esrei. One prepares with mehudar tzitzis and tefillin. Every word of the nusach, composed by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah with ruach hakodesh, brings a new tikkun each day, so each day's avodah cannot wait for tomorrow. Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, each word is a heichal, a palace; foreign thoughts mean being sent out of it, so one must daven slowly and with effort. The Rav discusses the pace of davening, the merit of guarding the bris, and enduring hardship for Hashem. Pesukei d'Zimra, from the word for cutting, cut through the destructive angels, and what was once optional has become an obligation in our weaker generation.

en: The aim of davening is to reach Shemoneh Esrei and stand before the King, passing on the way through the four worlds that the parts of davening correspond to.
One prepares to stand before the King with proper garments, chiefly tzitzis and tefillin, and the Rav urges getting mehudar ones even when they cost more.
Every word of tefillah was composed with ruach hakodesh so that each day it brings about a different tikkun, since every day and every person has a distinct task.
Each word of davening is a heichal; one must daven with effort and kavanah, saying Pesukei d'Zimra slowly like someone counting coins.
Tefillah is among the things that stand at the height of the world yet people treat lightly, as Dovid Hamelech already testified.
Pesukei d'Zimra cut a way through the atmosphere filled with destructive angels, because whoever goes along with Dovid Hamelech cannot be stopped.
Pesukei d'Zimra were once a voluntary practice of the pious and have become an obligation today, because our generation cannot rise in tefillah without them.

each word of tefillah as a heichal
Pesukei d'Zimra from voluntary to obligatory
angels and the ascent of prayer

title.en: Davening as a journey to the King

summary.en: The Rav announces that he now begins Pesukei d'Zimra and explains that the goal of davening is Shemoneh Esrei, standing before the King. To get there one passes through the four worlds: korbanos correspond to Asiyah, Pesukei d'Zimra to Yetzirah, the blessings of Shema to Beriah and Shemoneh Esrei to Atzilus.

title.en: Tzitzis and tefillin as royal garments

summary.en: Citing the Zera Kodesh, the Rav says one must prepare proper garments before entering the King, and the chief of these are tzitzis and tefillin, which raise a person and draw the Shechinah upon him. He urges buying mehudar tzitzis made lishmah and fine tefillin, even at extra cost.

title.en: A new tikkun every day

summary.en: The Rav explains that the words of davening, composed by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah with ruach hakodesh, bring a different tikkun each day, because the world rises daily toward its completion and every person has a unique task. With the Chiddushei HaRim's reading of 'if not now, when', he teaches that today's avodah cannot be pushed off to tomorrow.

title.en: Every word is a heichal

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, transmitted by the Chasam Sofer, that every word of davening is a heichal guarded by angels, and a foreign thought means being thrown out of it. Dovid Hamelech and the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah had keys to these palaces; Hashem in His mercy admits one who toils, so one must say Pesukei d'Zimra slowly, like counting precious coins.

title.en: How long to daven

summary.en: The Rav notes the poskim's measure of half an hour for Pesukei d'Zimra, tells of tzaddikim and of R' Avraham Ziskind who davened for hours, and of places like Kotzk and Belz where they davened quickly against the yetzer hara, which he says is not for us. He cites the Ba'al HaTanya's middle way and the Gemara's reading of 'kerum zulus livnei adam' as referring to tefillah, which people belittle.

title.en: The one who slays the serpent

summary.en: The Rav says one merits tefillah above all by guarding the bris, and brings the Zohar's mashal that whoever kills the serpent, the yetzer hara, receives the king's daughter, which is tefillah. Since today's street makes it nearly impossible to avoid sin, one must work harder and at least endure davening when it does not come easily.

title.en: Better to be broken before Hashem

summary.en: Every person must pass through suffering; with the Ohr HaChaim on 'mitachas sivlos Mitzrayim', the Rav explains that what one endures for Hashem is taken off other burdens. He brings his rebbe R' Feivel Mitlevitch's reading of 'al tikrei sivro ela shivro': since one must be broken anyway, better to be broken before Hashem, and one who trusts Him gains time for Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Cutting through the angels

summary.en: The Rav explains why he starts with Pesukei d'Zimra and, from the Shaarei Orah, describes the atmosphere between earth and heaven as filled with good and destructive angels that let prayers through or block them. 'Zimra' means cutting: by saying the psalms of Dovid Hamelech one goes along with him, and no one can stop him.

title.en: From voluntary practice to obligation

summary.en: The Rav shows from the Gemara that Pesukei d'Zimra were not originally an obligation, though saying them brings great merit, and asks why they are one today. Like the Tzemach Tzedek's answer about later stringencies, and like Maariv that became binding, our generation needs them: when the ketores purified the air prayers could rise, and without it we must say Pesukei d'Zimra. He closes by saying he will begin with Baruch She'amar next time.

catalogTitle: לשם יחוד וברוך שאמר

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the l'shem yichud said before Baruch She'amar, as a unification of Hashem with Klal Yisrael done in the name of all Jews, and then the first phrases of Baruch She'amar, showing that creation, Hashem's word and nature itself continue every moment according to the Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the l'shem yichud before Pesukei d'Zimra: its aim is to unite Hashem with His Shechinah dwelling in Klal Yisrael, with fear and love as the two wings that lift a mitzvah, and to complete Hashem's Name broken by Amalek. Saying it in the name of all Israel brings the deed into the world of Klal Yisrael, which no accusation reaches, like the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur. He then explains it as a moda'ah, a prior declaration that voids later stray thoughts, and tells of the Noda B'Yehuda's teshuva against saying it and the answers to it. Turning to Baruch She'amar, he explains that creation from nothing is renewed every moment, that Hashem is 'gozer u'mekayem' and never changes His mind, and that nature runs according to the Torah, changing as Jews add new chiddushim.

en: The l'shem yichud declares that a mitzvah is done to unite Hashem with His Shechinah in Klal Yisrael, like a groom with a bride, with fear and love.
A mitzvah done in the name of all Israel reaches the root of Klal Yisrael, where no accusation can reach and sins are erased, as on Yom Kippur.
Saying l'shem yichud before a mitzvah works like a moda'ah: a prior declaration that cancels foreign thoughts the yetzer hara may bring in during the mitzvah.
Creation is not a past event: Hashem's ten utterances still act every moment, and without them everything would cease.
'Baruch gozer u'mekayem' means that Hashem, who knows the future, never changes His mind, unlike a human ruler.
Nature runs according to the Torah, so when Jews add new chiddushim in Torah, Hashem renews nature accordingly.

candidateTopics: Hashem does not change His mind

title.en: What l'shem yichud means

summary.en: The Rav explains in simple terms the l'shem yichud said before Baruch She'amar: uniting Hashem with His Shechinah in Klal Yisrael with fear and love, the two wings without which a mitzvah cannot rise, and uniting the letters of Hashem's Name that are split because of Amalek.

title.en: In the name of all Israel

summary.en: The Rav explains why a mitzvah is done in the name of all Israel: the root world called Klal Yisrael is beyond any accusation, like the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur, which is why one must make peace before Yom Kippur and accept ahavas Yisrael before davening.

title.en: L'shem yichud as a moda'ah

summary.en: The Rav notes that the nusach comes from the early mekubalim and that the Ba'al HaTanya kept it in his siddur only before Baruch She'amar, then explains it as a moda'ah, like the declaration that voids a coerced get, which cancels stray thoughts during a mitzvah.

title.en: The Noda B'Yehuda and the early misnagdim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the first misnagdim were honest people who feared a new movement after the damage of Shabbatai Tzvi, tells of R' Shimon of Yaroslav and the stone-throwing misnaged, and relates that the Noda B'Yehuda wrote a teshuva against saying l'shem yichud, which the Sidduro shel Shabbos refuted; today it is accepted.

title.en: Baruch She'amar: creation renewed every moment

summary.en: The Rav turns to Baruch She'amar, which came down from heaven with eighty-seven words, and explains 'she'amar v'haya ha'olam' and 'omer v'oseh': creation from nothing is not history but goes on every second, shown with the meshalim of a power station's dynamos and a glass held in the hand.

title.en: Gozer u'mekayem: Hashem does not change His mind

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Hashem with politicians who break promises, explains that the One who knows the future cannot change His mind, uses this against religions that claim He gave a new law, grounding it in the mesorah from Sinai, and tells of a Rebbe exiled to Siberia who read 'gozer u'mekayem' about his own survival.

title.en: Oseh bereishis: nature follows the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'oseh bereishis': Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, so changes in the Torah's psak bring changes in the world, shown from R' Eliezer's town and from R' Chaim Ozer's advice to a sick man to move to Eretz Yisrael, where the Mechaber's ruling holds.

title.en: New chiddushim, new wonders in nature

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Avnei Nezer healing a sick man through a chiddush in Tosafos, brings that nature changes from generation to generation, and shows that the great flowering of Torah chiddushim in the Acharonim and in our day came together with great wonders in technology.

catalogTitle: ברוך מרחם על הארץ

oneLiner.en: Explaining the blessings 'Baruch merachem al ha'aretz', 'al habriyos', 'meshalem sachar tov' and 'podeh umatzil', the Rav shows that all of creation longs to return to Hashem, that Hashem's mercy and reward are pure kindness, and that above reward and punishment stands Hashem's way of redeeming even the undeserving.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'Baruch merachem al ha'aretz': Hashem has mercy even on the earth, because everything in creation, even plants and lifeless matter, has a longing. The world was built with chesed, which is love, and everything longs to return to its place; a piece of bread longs to be eaten with a brachah, and the hundred daily brachos counter forgetfulness. The earth, lowest of all, longs most to serve Hashem, which is why it is called eretz, from ratzon; the roads to Zion mourn because no pilgrims tread them. Dovid HaMelech too is called eretz. Turning to 'merachem al habriyos', the Rav teaches that a person who shows mercy, like Rebbi with the mouse, arouses mercy above. 'Meshalem sachar tov' praises Hashem for rewarding what no one deserves. Finally, 'podeh umatzil' describes a higher conduct than reward and punishment, seen in Yetzias Mitzrayim, Menashe's teshuvah and the extra verse after the aleph-beis of Tehillim 34.

en: Hashem has mercy even on the earth, because every part of creation, even plants and lifeless matter, has a longing, and above all a longing to return to Hashem.
The earth, the lowest level of creation and furthest from Hashem, has the strongest longing to serve Him; this is why it is called eretz, from ratzon.
A person who has mercy on Hashem's creatures arouses Hashem's mercy on himself, as Rebbi's suffering ended when he had pity on a mouse.
No one can repay Hashem for even one kindness, so all reward He gives, even for refraining from sin, is pure kindness and a praise of Hashem.
Besides the conduct of reward and punishment there is a higher conduct of pidyon, redemption, in which Hashem saves even those who do not deserve it, as a father with his children.
The season from Tu BiShvat until Shavuos is a time of this conduct of pidyon, when the days themselves are days of mercy.

title.en: The longing in all of creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem is merciful even to the earth because everything has a longing, even plants such as date palms, since the world was built with chesed. Everything longs to return to its place; bread longs to be eaten with a brachah, and the hundred daily brachos guard against the forgetfulness that rules up to a hundred.

title.en: Why the earth is called eretz

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Maggid saw fire lift the Ba'al Shem Tov's food to heaven, then explains that the earth, the lowest of creation, longs most to return to Hashem: eretz comes from ratzon. The roads to Zion mourn because pilgrims no longer tread them, so we ask Hashem to have mercy on the earth.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech as eretz; mercy on creatures

summary.en: The Rav notes that Dovid HaMelech, the last of the ushpizin, is called eretz, and discusses the Beis Yosef's question on the ending of the brachah of Boneh Yerushalayim, answered by Dovid being Yerushalayim. He then turns to 'merachem al habriyos': rain comes in the merit of animals, and he asks how a person merits Hashem's mercy.

title.en: Man's power above; Rebbi and the calf

summary.en: The Rav compares a person to a switch panel whose every act lights up the upper worlds, as with netilas yadayim in the Ramchal's Derech Hashem. He tells the Gemara's story of Rebbi, who suffered after sending away a calf that hid by him and was healed after having mercy on a mouse: mercy below arouses mercy above.

title.en: Meshalem sachar tov: reward as kindness

summary.en: On 'Baruch meshalem sachar tov lirei'av' the Rav brings the Chovos Halevavos and Nishmas: a whole life of mitzvos cannot repay one kindness, even one breath. So any reward is a gift; with the example of a driver who stops at a red light and expects no payment, he shows that Hashem rewards even refraining from sin.

title.en: Podeh umatzil and the season of redemption

summary.en: The Rav calls the weeks from Tu BiShvat to Shavuos a rising season full of Yomim Tovim, a time of pidyon. He explains that besides reward and punishment, the conduct of servants, Hashem has a higher conduct with His children, redeeming those who do not deserve it, which is the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.

title.en: Redemption beyond the rules

summary.en: The Rav shows the conduct of pidyon at Yetzias Mitzrayim, when Hashem redeemed the Jews despite the accusation at the Yam Suf, and with Menashe, whose teshuvah Hashem accepted through a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod. He applies it to the times set for Moshiach that the accuser spoiled, and says that at the time of redemption Hashem will not look at the accuser.

title.en: The verse beyond the aleph-beis

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Tzadok: Tehillim 34 and Tehillim 25 follow the aleph-beis, an order of reward and punishment, and each ends with an extra verse of pidyon outside that order. He explains 'nasati chofrecha Mitzrayim' through the angel created by a sin that must find its target, which Hashem sends to a rasha in place of the one doing teshuvah, the secret of kaparos.

catalogTitle: Emunah - Concealed Behind Layers of Rationalization and Impurity

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew inherits emunah from Avraham Avinu, and that a Jew who denies Hashem is only covering his inner belief with a layer of rationalization, which is what the word 'kofer' means.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the point of the previous week: a Jew has emunah by inheritance, the way a newborn instinctively knows how to nurse and a migrating bird finds its way back to the same tree, and the ba'al teshuvah's return to his roots shows it. He then asks why so many Jews declare that they do not believe. His answer is that they do believe, but disbelief is comfortable, so they suppress their emunah through rationalization. He explains rationalization with the fable of the wolf and the sour grapes, everyday examples, and the story of Chiel of Beis El, who explained away the death of his sons. He contrasts people driven by taivah, who do teshuvah in old age, with those driven by ga'avah, who never admit their mistake. He then explains Avraham Avinu as a new species that believes in Hashem, which is why the Avos were barren and why a hey was added to Avraham's name. Finally he explains that a kofer is one who covers over the truth, like the tar on Noach's ark.

en: Every Jew has emunah by inheritance from the Avos, like the knowledge animals and infants are born with rather than learn.
A Jew who declares that he does not believe is not telling the truth: he believes, but finds it comfortable not to, and suppresses his emunah.
Rationalization means that a person's ego will not let him admit his own fault, so he blames something else.
Whether a person does teshuvah in old age depends on whether his dominant drive is taivah or ga'avah.
Avraham Avinu was a new species, a human being who naturally believes in Hashem, and the hey added to his name gave him the power to continue that species.
A kofer is one who covers over a truth he knows inside; his heresy is only a veneer.

title.en: Emunah as an inherited instinct

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the children of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov have emunah by inheritance, and compares it to a newborn who knows how to nurse and a bird that finds its way back to the same tree. He sees the same instinct in ba'alei teshuvah returning to their roots.

title.en: Why do Jews deny? Rationalization

summary.en: The Rav asks why so many Jews say they do not believe, and answers that they do believe but suppress it, through the psychological law of rationalization. He notes that all of psychology is in the Torah, with the Chazon Ish's answer about psychology books, and explains rationalization with the fable of the wolf and the sour grapes.

title.en: Examples of rationalization: Chiel of Beis El

summary.en: The Rav gives everyday examples of blaming something else, a bochur who blames the lighting and an inexperienced sukkah builder who blames the hammer, and then tells how Chiel of Beis El rebuilt Yericho despite Yehoshua's curse and found an excuse for the death of each son.

title.en: Taivah, ga'avah and teshuvah in old age

summary.en: After the bird that hides its head in the sand, the Rav describes old people in a nursing home who return to Yiddishkeit once they can no longer indulge, and explains that those driven by taivah do teshuvah while those driven by ga'avah never admit their life was folly. A weak person who does not want to fight his yetzer says the fault is in religion.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, a new species of believer

summary.en: The Rav says that a professed atheist really believes, because every Jew inherits the emunah of Avraham Avinu, of whom the Torah first says that he believed in Hashem. He explains that Avraham was a new species, severed from the previous generations, which is why he was barren and needed the hey added to his name, as with Sarah and Bilhah.

title.en: A kofer covers over the truth

summary.en: The Rav sums up that the believing Jew is a new kind of being, which is why the Avos had to be barren. He then explains that 'kofer' means one who covers over a truth he knows, like the kofer (tar) smeared on Noach's ark and the kapores covering the aron, and concludes that every Jew believes deep down, as believers the children of believers.
